entries.title: Motion Design UI Morphing Animation
entries.description: A highly detailed prompt for creating an 11-second motion design video showing UI state morphs using code-generated animations.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the accent colour, a song (mp3), the words for the 3 text moments (search query, card title, toast). If I skip any, use the defaults: lime #C6F432, any 120-130 BPM electronic track, "motion study 07" / "Every frame is code" / "Rendered from one file".
</inputs>

<direction>
One black shape (#0e0e10) on a warm light stage (#f4f4f1 to #e1e1dc radial). It never cuts: every UI state is born out of the one before it. White text, Geist for UI, Geist Mono for numbers and labels. The accent appears only where something turns on.
A macOS cursor drives every change with real clicks and one real drag.
Every morph uses one curve: cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1). Pop-ins use a closed-form spring with a tiny overshoot. Text rises through a mask line, it never fades in.
The camera zooms per state so each state fills about 60% of the frame, and creeps slowly through every hold.
Banned: crossfades, hard cuts, bouncy easing, particles, glows, gradients on UI chrome, holds over 1 second, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM grid, 24 beats, then the whole film is time-warped onto the real song's beat.
Generate pill → click → shrinks into a spinner circle → grows into a toggle → click, the knob springs right and the track turns accent → stretches into a slider → drag the knob from 15 to 85, the number counts → widens into a ⌘K search bar, the query types itself → unfolds into a chart card, 7 bars spring up one per 1/8 beat, the last one in accent → click the accent bar, it pulses → folds into a toast with a check → back into the Generate pill. Last frame = first frame, cursor included.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state between frames.
2. The shape is one div. Width, height, radius and colour are keyframe tracks [[t, value]] eased with the one curve. Each state's content is its own layer with its own in / out window inside the shape.
3. Camera: one scale track around the centre, plus a 1.2% sine creep over the whole loop.
4. Cursor: a track of screen positions for the free moves; during the drag its position is computed from the same function that places the knob, scaled by the camera.
5. Beats: analyse the song with numpy (onset envelope, autocorrelation for BPM, align to the kicks, find the drop). Put the drop on the chart bars springing up.
6. Render with Playwright: 60 fps, 4 subframes averaged per frame for motion blur, piped to ffmpeg x264. Then one real SFX per event (click, select, typing, whoosh), placed by its measured peak, quiet under the music, loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
</build>

entries.title: Explodable Pencil Sharpener Mechanism
entries.description: A prompt to create an interactive 3D model of a manual pencil sharpener using Three.js, allowing users to take it apart to see gears, cutters, and springs. Includes specific mechanical details like tooth counts and cutting angles.
entries.prompt:
I wish someone had taught me physics this way!

I've always wondered how a manual crank pencil sharpener manages to create such a perfectly sharp point.

So I asked Claude Opus 5.5 to build one I could literally take apart and explore.

Here's how it works:

«It recreated the entire sharpener from a single reference image, with every gear, cutter, and spring built using Three.js.»

«Turn the crank, and both cutters rotate around the pencil while a fixed 36-tooth ring drives each cutter's rotation.»

«Each cutter has 15 helical edges. That's 12 rotations and 1,080 individual cuts, producing a precise 22° pencil point before the crank suddenly becomes lighter.»

«Pull out the drawer, and you can see the cedar shavings collected inside the transparent acrylic compartment.»

This is such a brilliant way to understand how everyday mechanisms work.

I turned the entire process into a Claude skill, so you can recreate this experience using almost any reference image.

The free skill and all the prompts are in the article below. 👇

entries.title: Disassembling Robot Squid Animation
entries.description: A prompt to create a detailed 3D robot squid in Three.js from a single reference image. The animation features complex mechanics like logarithmic spiral arms, visor lifting, and an explosion/reassembly sequence.
entries.prompt:
The reference image determined the design, but every plate, roller, and lens was built directly in Three.js.

Opus generated its own still image, compared it against the reference, and refined the differences across 6 rounds before rendering a single frame.

The first version had a sail-like fin on the mantle. I removed it and replaced its function with a visor that lifts off using 4 pins.

154 individual links spread across 8 arms, each progressively smaller so the tips curl into a logarithmic spiral.

Starting at 0:03, a new component detaches with every beat: the iris, visor, an arm, mantle window, and siphon.

At 0:16, the entire squid explodes into separate components during a 330° spin, reassembles at 0:19, then jets out of the frame.

entries.title: AAA Quality Rendering Pipeline in Three.js
entries.description: A detailed guide/prompt for building a physically-based rendering pipeline in Three.js capable of AAA game quality visuals. Includes FFT ocean, atmospheric scattering, global illumination, volumetric fog/clouds, and tone mapping techniques.
entries.prompt:
Build a physically-based real-time rendering pipeline in Three.js to achieve AAA game/movie quality visuals.
Components:
- FFT Ocean simulation.
- Physical Atmosphere scattering.
- Global Illumination (GI).
- Volumetric Clouds and Fog.
- GTAO (Ground Truth Ambient Occlusion).
- Auto Exposure and Local Tone Mapping.

Workflow:
1. Establish the physical base (materials/lighting values).
2. Apply stylization via parameters (time-of-day, weather, post-processing).
3. Use reference images (from actual AAA games/movies) to fit parameters.
4. Optimize using least squares method to minimize difference between rendered output and reference measurements (brightness, saturation, hue).

entries.prompt:

entries.title: Night Shift 3D Cartoon Animation
entries.description: A detailed prompt/workflow description for creating a 25-second 3D cartoon animation 'Night Shift' using Opus 5.5 and Three.js.
entries.prompt: Introducing Night Shift: a 25 second 3D cartoon where Claude gets buried in 4,812 orders, then automates the whole shift. 1 HTML file + 0 keyframes + 6 minutes of render = 25 seconds at 60 fps. The story in 4 beats: → 2:00 AM, the belt speeds up and the board climbs from 120 to 480 units an hour → a box lands on Clawd's head, the belt jams, the pile buries everything but the eyes → Clawd bursts out, types claude into a terminal, two robot arms wake up and sort every box into its zone on the beat → 6:00 AM, dawn through the skylight, Clawd in a hammock with coffee, the board reads SHIFT DONE. Step 1 → Claude Opus 5.5 writes the whole scene in Three.js inside Claude Code, one renderAt(t) function draws any frame from the time alone. Step 2 → the belt speed is integrated every 10 ms. Step 3 → the robot arms use 2-joint inverse kinematics. Step 4 → the quota board, the terminal and the clock are live canvas textures. Step 5 → the soundtrack is synthesized. Step 6 → headless Chrome renders 3,000 frames at 120 fps, ffmpeg blends them to 60 fps with motion blur.

entries.translated_prompt:
Build a painted 3D world in the browser using Three.js.

Every frame should look painted, and as the sun sets, the style transitions from gouache to oil paint.

- Step 8: Animate a camera path along the planned walk, synchronizing the movement with the setting sun.

Role distribution:

> Three.js handles the rendering of the 3D world.
> The paint shader ensures the output resembles a physical painting.
> The user evaluates each frame based on artistic merit rather than gaming mechanics.

entries.title: Detailed Prompt for Calisthenics Animation with Claude Opus 5.5
entries.description: A comprehensive, reusable prompt for generating a flat cartoon explainer video using Python and Skia-python rendered via ffmpeg. It specifies character sprite extraction from a reference sheet, posing logic, timing sync with voiceover, color palettes, and scene composition rules.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the topic (default: how peptides work), the length (default 60 seconds), whether I want captions on screen (default yes), and whether I have my own sound effects (if not, synthesize them in numpy). I attach the red character sheet on a black background. After I answer, write a voiceover script of about 2.4 words per second, give it to me in a code block, then stop and wait for my voiceover audio before you render anything.
</inputs>

<direction>
A flat cartoon explainer short at 1080x1920, 30fps, drawn entirely in code with Python and skia-python, piped to ffmpeg, one encoded file per scene joined with the concat demuxer. Every shape anti-aliased.
Character: cut each pose out of the attached sheet into its own transparent sprite. The background is black and so are the outlines, so flood-fill the background from the image edges only at low tolerance and keep all black inside the figure (outlines, sleeves, waistband). Keep the white eyes. Add a 3px navy #24364F stroke around each silhouette to replace the lost edge. Upscale 3x with Lanczos. Show me a contact sheet of the cut-outs on #D3DFEC before going further.
Posing: the character is a presenter anchored to the bottom edge, 800-1050px wide, never floating. Pick the pose from the line being spoken: pointing at the viewer for the hook and the final line, finger up when explaining, shrug on a question, arms crossed while watching, open palm when presenting an object, pointing at a zoom bubble. 1 to 3 pose changes per scene. Each change lands with a squash and stretch over 9 frames (8% wider, 10% shorter, then back). Idle: 0.5 degree sway and a 0.6% breathing scale.
Script: a hook question in the first 4 seconds, a title line, 4 to 5 beats that each carry one visual idea, a one-line payoff. Short sentences, plain words, every claim accurate, no medical advice.
Timing: run silencedetect on my voiceover at -35dB, 0.22s. Cut scenes in the middle of the long pauses and fire every pop, label and pose change on the word it belongs to.
Palette: backgrounds pale blue #D3DFEC, mid blue #B4C7E6, strong blue #6790CB. Outlines and text navy #24364F. Accents amber #F4B740, coral #EE7B5B, teal #58B7A8, lilac #9A86D6. Flat fills only, 5-9px navy outlines on every drawn object.
Scenes: the title card is solid #37557F with two lines of white text sliding in from opposite sides and an amber underline. At least two close-up scenes with no character. One circular zoom bubble, 320px radius, white ring with navy edges, that the character points at. The final scene is #6790CB with 14 lighter rotating rays.
Diagrams: every explainer visual is drawn in code from circles, rounded rectangles and lines: chains of beads joined by a thick navy link, cells with a dotted membrane, arrows as moving dashed lines, labels in white rounded pills with a 6px navy outline.
Captions: Inter ExtraBold Italic, all capitals, 66px, navy, centred at the top between y=200 and y=340, two lines maximum, each line rising 24px and fading in over 9 frames on its word. White with a navy stroke on the strong blue scene.
Movement: a slow push-in from 100% to 104% across every scene, 14 soft white particles drifting upward at 35% opacity, every new element popping in with an 18% overshoot, beads rippling in a wave, a 7% zoom punch on the final line.
Draw order: background, particles, floor line, diagrams, character, captions on top.
Sound: my voiceover at full level. Effects at half the voice level: a swoosh 0.12s before each cut, a whip on each pose change, a pop on each element, a click or chime on key moments, a low hit on the title card and the final line.
Before the full render: render 14 still frames at the busiest moments, look at them, fix overlaps and text leaving the frame.
Banned: gradients, drop shadows, glow, 3D, AI images or AI video, stock footage, music, emojis, watermarks, any character other than the attached one, any other channel's characters, logo or name, text smaller than 30px, a character that floats above the bottom edge, more than two caption lines.
</direction>

entries.title: Clay Stop Motion Film Workflow
entries.description: Detailed workflow for creating a clay-style stop motion film about Information Security Management using Opus 5.5, Blender, and Remotion.
entries.prompt:
7 days. One laptop. A GTX 1660 Ti with 6GB VRAM and 7.7GB usable RAM.

41,562 frames. 28 minutes, 51 seconds.

Been working nonstop with opus 5.5 max on a clay-style stop motion film about Information Security Management and it's finally finished.

The idea was to create something visually closer to wallace & gromit than a conventional corporate training presentation. Clay-style characters, minimature looking sets, cinematic camera movements, expressive performances, a little humor and an actual story.

The film runs at 24fps but is animated on twos, meaning 12 visual updates per sec, giving it that deliberate handmade stop motion feel. 

The entire production was done on my laptop. No render farm and roughly 33 hours spent rendering on the 1660 Ti alone.

For anyone interested in how it was made, here's the actual workflow:

1) Blender: 3d characters, environments, animation, miniature style lighting and a cinematic camera work.

2) Remotion: scene composition, editing, transitions, subtitles, title cards and motion graphics.

3) FFmpeg: video processing, encoding and final assembly.

4) Sarvam Bulbul: 291 dialogue lines across five character voices.

5) ElevenLabs: 76 additional dialogue lines, including an italian accented character.

6) Earshot: auditioning, evaluating, and ranking voice takes before selecting the performances.

7) Poly Haven & BlenderKit: materials, textures, props and assets for the 3d environments.

8) Pexels: additional visual elements, including rain footage.

9) Custom lettering engine: a 68-glyph hand drawn alphabet built from strokes because regular fonts didn't quite capture the aesthetic i wanted.

Opus 5.5 max was my primary development collaborator throughout the week, haiku 5.5 xhigh helped inspect rendered frames, gpt 6.1 terra max reviewed the film because i wanted it's vision capability lastly deepseek v4.1 flash 1017 and hy4 assisted with subsequent review passes.

A fair amount of time went into debugging renders, refining character movements, adjusting lighting and camera angles, reviewing dialogue and checking how everything came together and was completed the day before fable 5.2 launched lol.

The project actually started as an information security awareness film for my father's company in India, the goal was to help employees understand security concepts through storytelling rather than another conventional training presentations.

As the film developed, i realised it could be useful beyond its original audience, so i decided to share it publicly as well :)

The full film is attached below. I'd appreciate any thoughts literally anything!

and don't skip the ending, there's a post cred scene ;)

entries.title: Photorealistic 3D Film Workflow
entries.description: Workflow for creating a photorealistic 3D film 'River of Lanterns' using Claude Code, Three.js, and Opus 5.5.
entries.prompt:
Photorealistic 3D production challenge,
I created the 30-second 3D video "Lantern River" using only Claude Code (Three.js).

[AI Team Production]
Director: Claude Fable 5.2
Assistants: Opus 5.5 x 5 units
Inspector: Sonnet 5.5

[Tools Used]
- Claude Code
- Three.js (Browser 3D. No assets, all code)
- Running Chrome headless to screenshot one command at a time → converted to video with ffmpeg
- Sound: Stable Audio 3 running on my own PC (music) + Python for synthesis (fire, bell, fireworks, insects, water)
- Did not use any paid image, video, or sound generation
- Graphics board is RTX 3060

[What I Did]
- Wrote design documents and work plans
- Director creates the foundation (world map, camera path, rendering direction, output and inspection tools)
- 5 assistants create parts in parallel (6000 lanterns, water surface and shore, 345 houses, sky and fireworks, music and sound effects)
- Repeated one command 32 to 128 times to render, creating rhythm and pin drops of movement
- Water surface renders by re-rendering the world backwards once more
- Had the inspector who doesn't know the premise watch the still images 4 times, asked "what does the final form look like?", and fixed it based on that
- Made the initial blurry fire and the view of the street lights from above at the end have the same shape
- Full HD, 900-command output takes about 6 minutes. Code is about 5,400 lines
- From starting to write code to completion, took about 2 hours and 10 minutes

entries.prompt: 画面是一条巨型锦鲤翱翔在黄昏云海之上，它的背上完整承载着一座日式小庭院：包含茶室、池塘、红桥、樱花树、石灯笼与鸟居。池塘的水向外溢出，顺着鱼身化作瀑布滴落进云层；鱼鳍与鱼尾随风摆动，樱花花瓣不断向后飘散，仙鹤伴飞，搭配黄昏柔光、柔和阴影与电影感环绕镜头，细节非常丰富。
entries.translated_prompt: The scene features a giant koi fish soaring above twilight sea clouds. On its back sits a complete small Japanese garden: including a tea room, pond, red bridge, cherry blossom trees, stone lanterns, and torii gates. Water from the pond overflows, cascading down the fish's body as waterfalls into the clouds; fins and tail sway in the wind, cherry blossom petals drift backward continuously, cranes fly alongside, accompanied by soft twilight lighting, gentle shadows, and cinematic orbiting camera angles, with rich details.

entries.title: Code-Generated Animal Animation with Precision Checks
entries.description: A workflow for creating code-driven animal animations (like a crab) using Claude Opus 5.5, where the model uses a reference image as a target and enforces strict geometric proportions via a checklist rather than guessing textures.
entries.prompt: Build a crab animation from one picture. Use the picture as a target, never a texture. Create a checklist for that one picture, including the word "never" to enforce constraints. Count dark pixels against the reference; pass at 0.80 similarity. Measure proportions off the picture, not guessed. The whole film is one script file; a new cut is one edited line. Ensure every shell, gear and claw is generated by code.

entries.title: Disney's 12 Principles of Animation Prompt
entries.description: A reusable prompt structure applying Disney's 12 principles of animation to guide Claude Opus 5.5 in creating smooth, character-driven HTML/Canvas animations, moving beyond robotic movement.
entries.prompt: Apply the following 12 principles to animate the character: 00 First try: make Clawd jump onto the other box. 01 Arcs: move him along a curve, never a straight line. 02 Slow in & out: let him hang at the top, ease in and out of it. 03 Squash & stretch: stretch on take-off, squash on landing, same volume. 04 Anticipation: crouch down first, so we see the jump coming. 05 Follow-through: arms and legs drag behind and settle after he lands. 06 Timing: hold the crouch a beat, then snap off fast. 07 Solid drawing: lean him into the arc so he has weight. 08 Secondary action: eyes on the landing spot, arms flap for balance. 09 Pose to pose: key 5 poses: crouch, launch, apex, contact, settle. 10 Staging: low 3/4 camera, light on him, dim the rest. 11 Exaggeration: jump twice as high and throw in a flip. 12 Appeal: stick the landing, then a little ta-da.

entries.title: Glitch Title Animation Prompt
entries.description: A specific prompt for Claude Opus 5.5 to build a glitch title effect in code (Python/ffmpeg) with customizable text and colors.
entries.prompt:
Build a glitch title effect in code (Python/ffmpeg). [16:9, 1920x1080, 30fps, 10 s, with sound]

Text: "{argument name="word" default="WORD"}", {argument name="text_color" default="white"}, {argument name="font_name" default="Arial"}, dark drop shadow underneath.
Loop (x4): letters flash one at a time in their own slots within the word (2 frames each) →
full word appears with a slight jitter and occasional glitches → disappears by {argument name="exit_effect" default="glitching apart"}.

Background: dark base with bright, saturated, broken vertical scan lines and downward-dripping streaks;
dark areas stay as black silhouettes. Generate it from the attached images. Mix in striped ring/polygon scenes.
Hard cut every 2–4 frames, never repeating.
On top: horizontal slice shifts, RGB split, light grain. Colors: {argument name="colors" default="red + cyan"}.

Story (optional): {argument name="story_summary" default="short summary"} — each loop is one chapter; colors, images and the exit effect match it.
Deliver: MP4 + script.

entries.title: Kinetic Typography Film: Data Center Costs
entries.description: A comprehensive prompt for creating a 25-second kinetic typography film explaining data center electricity costs, featuring specific visual metaphors like erasers on architectural drawings and distinct material styles (graphite, steel, ink).
entries.prompt: Create a 25.00-second kinetic typography film titled **“WHO PAYS FOR THE WIRES?”**  Make it for someone opening an electric bill at their kitchen table. They should finish the film able to explain why a data center can cost money before it uses electricity, and who bears one specific construction risk in AEP Ohio’s service territory.  Deliver one self-contained HTML file with original stereo sound, embedded artwork and type, a 1920 × 1080 capture area, and deterministic 60fps rendering. Give the film the craft of an opening title sequence and the factual precision of a reported graphic.  **The shot to build first**  An eraser sweeps across an architectural drawing. In twelve frames it can remove a building big enough to fill the screen. At the edge of the site, the eraser collides with a steel transmission tower that has already been erected. The pencil shaft flexes. The graphite tip breaks against the paper as the pencil falls. The steel gives one low, sustained note.  Hold on the empty site and the standing tower. Let the viewer discover the question a beat before the words arrive.  Everything before this shot prepares the distinction between *planned* and *built*. Everything after it follows the cost of what remains.  **One world, three materials**  Build a single tabletop set. An opened utility envelope, a household bill, a translucent engineering drawing, and a contract occupy different depths. Behind the table, one warm kitchen window establishes a human scale. Keep the household bill anonymous and its dollar amount outside the crop.  Use graphite for proposed work. A soft mark can be drawn, smeared, or erased. Use dull galvanized steel for installed infrastructure. It casts a hard shadow and has real mass. Use dark red ink for financial obligations. It moves through the contract and invoice while the steel stays planted on the site.  Set the headlines in a heavy, slightly narrow grotesque. Set the contract paraphrase in a readable book serif. The type should look like it belongs to the surface carrying it. During a fast move, one word can become architecture. During its reading hold, give the viewer its complete silhouette.  **0.00–3.00 seconds · The envelope**  Start in near darkness. Paper slides across wood. A kitchen light catches the embossed words **ELECTRIC BILL**. One thumb holds the envelope against the table while a finger opens the fold. Give the paper a little resistance. The sound is close enough to hear the fibers separate.  From this low angle, the fold makes a roofline. Move along it until a printed rule on the bill meets a survey line on the translucent plan underneath. Follow that line into the plan. In the margin, establish **ILLUSTRATIVE PROJECT**. The site and cancellation are a hypothetical example.  **3.00–7.50 seconds · Build two different futures**  Reveal **PROPOSED DATA CENTER** in graphite. The crossbars of the letters extend into a floor plan. Rack aisles draw themselves in quick succession. Leave a small square gap at the far end of the building. The viewer will recognize that patch of bare paper after the erasure.  In the foreground, the phrase **GRID WORK BEGINS** lands. Use the strokes of GRID as fabrication guides. Steel members lift off the guides, rotate around visible joints, and bolt into a single tower. Give the tower one distinctive asymmetrical gusset plate. A cable settles into its insulator with a short downward sag.  Keep both states readable in one low tracking shot. Behind the tower, a building still made of pencil. In front, steel already casting a shadow. The score borrows its rhythm from the work. Two bolt strikes, a cable pluck, a pencil stroke. Build the bass underneath those sounds.  **7.50–11.50 seconds · Cancel the project**  Across the top edge of the drawing, typeset **WHAT IF THE DEVELOPER CANCELS?** Let CANCELS travel with the eraser while the rest of the question holds steady.  Execute the pencil shot. Give the disappearing rack lines a dry directional smear. Let the last graphite dust settle around the tower footing. The kitchen light keeps shining through the same window. The audience should feel the peculiar ordinariness of a project that simply stops.  Land **BEFORE POWER IS SWITCHED ON** beside the empty site. A small service switch, previously visible on the plan margin, stays open. Omit the server-fan crescendo the score has led us to expect. Leave the steel ringing.  **11.50–15.00 seconds · Find the cost**  Lock the camera for half a second. Across the vacant footprint, place **THE WIRES ARE ALREADY UP.**  Then lower the camera until the tower’s diagonal brace fills the frame. Follow its shadow across the paper. The shadow meets a red invoice rule at precisely the same angle. Move from one to the other in a continuous shot. The solid tower remains visible behind us in the reflection of a metal ruler.  Reveal **WHO PAYS?** Set WHO small enough to fit between the strokes of the monumental P in PAYS. Let the question mark land over the original envelope. Hold the empty space beneath it. This is where a viewer might expect to see their own name.  **15.00–20.50 seconds · Read the agreement**  Slide the translucent drawing aside. Beneath it is the contract that has been on the table since the opening. A red rule leads to the source label **AEP OHIO · DATA CENTER AGREEMENT**. Present the operative condition in editorial type, clearly identified as a paraphrase.  Use three successive reading holds.  **CUSTOMER CANCELS BEFORE POWER-UP**  **DATA CENTER CUSTOMER REIMBURSES THE UTILITY**  **100% OF BUILDOUT COSTS**  Keep the condition and the AEP Ohio label visible when **100%** lands. Give **OF BUILDOUT COSTS** enough room to read at the same glance as the number. That wording defines exactly what the percentage covers.  Build the percentage sign from objects already on the table. Two punched registration holes supply the circles. The camera slides until the tower brace aligns between them to form the slash. The viewpoint clicks into place and **100%** reads as a single piece of typography. Hold it for at least 1.4 seconds. A viewer who pauses here should get a complete, accurately qualified frame.  Sound the answer with the same three notes heard during construction, now tapped on the desk with a pencil. Let the final note coincide with the registration of the percent sign.  **20.50–25.00 seconds · Return to the kitchen**  Pull back. The household bill occupies the near side of the table. Across from it, the project invoice sits on the developer’s agreement. The red obligation line ends there. Between the two documents stands the same tower, its gusset plate catching the kitchen light.  The final copy belongs in the empty building footprint.  **WHO PAYS FOR THE WIRES?**   **IN THIS OHIO CASE, THE DATA CENTER CUSTOMER.**  Hold this composition from approximately 21.7 to 24.2 seconds. Finish with the sound of the pencil stub rolling across the table and coming to rest against the tower footing. The kitchen light goes out. Reach black by 24.85 seconds.  **Sound and pacing**  Write the score at 144 BPM, giving 15 bars in 25 seconds. Let construction sounds push against the beat. Place the pencil break between beats so it feels like an interruption. Reserve the strongest bass resonance for the standing tower after the project disappears. A quieter, closer kitchen sound at the end should make the return to the household tangible.  Generate the full score and effects as one original 48 kHz stereo buffer, exactly 1,200,000 samples per channel. Drive playback from the audio clock. Use the same cue records for the bolt landings, eraser contact, pencil break, percentage alignment, and their sounds.  **Reporting and delivery**  Use the cancellation provision in AEP Ohio’s Letter of Agreement as the factual basis. Its trigger in this example is customer cancellation before the target energizati

Give the film the craft of an opening title sequence and the factual precision of a reported graphic.

**The shot to build first**
An eraser sweeps across an architectural drawing. In twelve frames it can remove a building big enough to fill the screen. At the edge of the site, the eraser collides with a steel transmission tower that has already been erected. The pencil shaft flexes. The graphite tip breaks against the paper as the pencil falls. The steel gives one low, sustained note.
Hold on the empty site and the standing tower. Let the viewer discover the question a beat before the words arrive.
Everything before this shot prepares the distinction between planned and built. Everything after it follows the cost of what remains.

**One world, three materials**
Build a single tabletop set. An opened utility envelope, a household bill, a translucent engineering drawing, and a contract occupy different depths. Behind the table, one warm kitchen window establishes a human scale. Keep the household bill anonymous and its dollar amount outside the crop.
Use graphite for proposed work. A soft mark can be drawn, smeared, or erased. Use dull galvanized steel for installed infrastructure. It casts a hard shadow and has real mass. Use dark red ink for financial obligations. It moves through the contract and invoice while the steel stays planted on the site.
Set the headlines in a heavy, slightly narrow grotesque. Set the contract paraphrase in a readable book serif. The type should look like it belongs to the surface carrying it. During a fast move, one word can become architecture. During its reading hold, give the viewer its complete silhouette.

**0.00–3.00 seconds · The envelope**
Start in near darkness. Paper slides across wood. A kitchen light catches the embossed words ELECTRIC BILL. One thumb holds the envelope against the table while a finger opens the fold. Give the paper a little resistance. The sound is close enough to hear the fibers separate.
From this low angle, the fold makes a roofline. Move along it until a printed rule on the bill meets a survey line on the translucent plan underneath. Follow that line into the plan. In the margin, establish ILLUSTRATIVE PROJECT. The site and cancellation are a hypothetical example.

**3.00–7.50 seconds · Build two different futures**
Reveal PROPOSED DATA CENTER in graphite. The crossbars of the letters extend into a floor plan. Rack aisles draw themselves in quick succession. Leave a small square gap at the far end of the building. The viewer will recognize that patch of bare paper after the erasure.
In the foreground, the phrase GRID WORK BEGINS lands. Use the strokes of GRID as fabrication guides. Steel members lift off the guides, rotate around visible joints, and bolt into a single tower. Give the tower one distinctive asymmetrical gusset plate. A cable settles into its insulator with a short downward sag.
Keep both states readable in one low tracking shot. Behind the tower, a building still made of pencil. In front, steel already casting a shadow. The score borrows its rhythm from the work. Two bolt strikes, a cable pluck, a pencil stroke. Build the bass underneath those sounds.

**7.50–11.50 seconds · Cancel the project**
Across the top edge of the drawing, typeset WHAT IF THE DEVELOPER CANCELS? Let CANCELS travel with the eraser while the rest of the question holds steady.
Execute the pencil shot. Give the disappearing rack lines a dry directional smear. Let the last graphite dust settle around the tower footing. The kitchen light keeps shining through the same window. The audience should feel the peculiar ordinariness of a project that simply stops.
Land BEFORE POWER IS SWITCHED ON beside the empty site. A small service switch, previously visible on the plan margin, stays open. Omit the server-fan crescendo the score has led us to expect. Leave the steel ringing.

**11.50–15.00 seconds · Find the cost**
Lock the camera for half a second. Across the vacant footprint, place THE WIRES ARE ALREADY UP.
Then lower the camera until the tower’s diagonal brace fills the frame. Follow its shadow across the paper. The shadow meets a red invoice rule at precisely the same angle. Move from one to the other in a continuous shot. The solid tower remains visible behind us in the reflection of a metal ruler.
Reveal WHO PAYS? Set WHO small enough to fit between the strokes of the monumental P in PAYS. Let the question mark land over the original envelope. Hold the empty space beneath it. This is where a viewer might expect to see their own name.

**15.00–20.50 seconds · Read the agreement**
Slide the translucent drawing aside. Beneath it is the contract that has been on the table since the opening. A red rule leads to the source label AEP OHIO · DATA CENTER AGREEMENT. Present the operative condition in editorial type, clearly identified as a paraphrase.
Use three successive reading holds.
CUSTOMER CANCELS BEFORE POWER-UP
DATA CENTER CUSTOMER REIMBURSES THE UTILITY
100% OF BUILDOUT COSTS
Keep the condition and the AEP Ohio label visible when 100% lands. Give OF BUILDOUT COSTS enough room to read at the same glance as the number. That wording defines exactly what the percentage covers.
Build the percentage sign from objects already on the table. Two punched registration holes supply the circles. The camera slides until the tower brace aligns between them to form the slash. The viewpoint clicks into place and 100% reads as a single piece of typography. Hold it for at least 1.4 seconds. A viewer who pauses here should get a complete, accurately qualified frame.
Sound the answer with the same three notes heard during construction, now tapped on the desk with a pencil. Let the final note coincide with the registration of the percent sign.

**20.50–25.00 seconds · Return to the kitchen**
Pull back. The household bill occupies the near side of the table. Across from it, the project invoice sits on the developer’s agreement. The red obligation line ends there. Between the two documents stands the same tower, its gusset plate catching the kitchen light.
The final copy belongs in the empty building footprint.
WHO PAYS FOR THE WIRES?
IN THIS OHIO CASE, THE DATA CENTER CUSTOMER.
Hold this composition from approximately 21.7 to 24.2 seconds. Finish with the sound of the pencil stub rolling across the table and coming to rest against the tower footing. The kitchen light goes out. Reach black by 24.85 seconds.

**Sound and pacing**
Write the score at 144 BPM, giving 15 bars in 25 seconds. Let construction sounds push against the beat. Place the pencil break between beats so it feels like an interruption. Reserve the strongest bass resonance for the standing tower after the project disappears. A quieter, closer kitchen sound at the end should make the return to the household tangible.
Generate the full score and effects as one original 48 kHz stereo buffer, exactly 1,200,000 samples per channel. Drive playback from the audio clock. Use the same cue records for the bolt landings, eraser contact, pencil break, percentage alignment, and their sounds.

**Reporting and delivery**
Use the cancellation provision in AEP Ohio’s Letter of Agreement as the factual basis. Its trigger in this example is customer cancellation before the target energizati

entries.title: Realistic Desert Simulation in Godot with Physics
entries.description: A prompt for creating a realistic desert environment in Godot 4 using GPU compute shaders, featuring physics-based dune formation via the Werner model, interactive footprints, and particle-based sand blowing.
entries.prompt:
Godot 4（Forward+）で、物理で動くリアルな砂漠を作って。計算はGPUのcompute shaderで。
地形は「高さの格子」を3段重ね
・遠景：約1km四方を0.5m格子
・中景：約33m四方を1.6cm格子
・足元：キャラクターに追従する約4m四方を2mm格子
・細かい層の内側では粗い層を描かない（継ぎ目のちらつき防止）

砂丘は描かずに、風で育てる（Werner型モデル）
・512m周期の領域を0.5m格子で、3000ステップ
・毎ステップ：風上の高い所から10〜15°の「風の影」に入っていないマスから砂を少し持ち上げ、約4m風下に落とす
・影の中には必ず積もる。砂の上は積もりやすく、むき出しの地面は積もりにくい
・33°より急な斜面は崩す
・最後に稜線を少し丸め、滑落面を31〜33°に。結果はキャッシュ
足跡と崩れ
・靴底の形で高さを押し下げ、押しのけた分を縁に盛る（体積保存）
・毎フレーム、急すぎる分だけ8近傍へ砂を流す。止まった砂は34°、流れ出したら28°まで崩れる
・湿った砂は崩れにくくする

舞い上がる砂
・削った体積とまったく同じ量を粒子にして飛ばし、着地したら整数アトミックで高さに足し戻す（砂の総量は不変）
・重力＋空気抵抗＋風
・粉塵は3層（濃い芯／外側／長く漂う層）、自己影と地形の影つき
見た目（自作シェーダ）
・法線＝高さ＋波長と向きの違う風紋2つをノイズで混ぜる＋ピクセルサイズの粒の凹凸
・拡散はd'EonのLambert-sphere＋Hapke
・影には空の青い光と、周りの日向からの暖かい照り返し
・きらめき：ワールドに固定した1px未満の点を、太陽と視線のハーフベクトルが風紋の法線に近い所だけ光らせる（太陽側に光の帯ができる）
・セルフシャドウは高さ場のレイマーチ
光とカメラ
・低い太陽（13〜16°）を風下側に置き、稜線で光と影を分ける
・空気遠近の霧を数層
・動画は120fpsで書き出し、4フレームを線形光で平均して30fps（自然なモーションブラー）
entries.translated_prompt:
Create a realistic desert simulation in Godot 4 (Forward+) where movement is driven by physics. Perform calculations on the GPU using compute shaders.
Terrain consists of three stacked layers of height grids:
- Far view: ~1km square with 0.5m grid
- Mid view: ~33m square with 1.6cm grid
- Foot level: ~4m square following the character with 2mm grid
- Do not render coarse layers inside fine layers (to prevent seam flickering)

Grow dunes with wind instead of drawing them (Werner-type model):
- Area with 512m period at 0.5m grid, 3000 steps
- Each step: Lift sand slightly from cells not in the "wind shadow" (10-15° angle) from higher upwind areas, drop it ~4m downwind
- Sand always accumulates in shadows. It accumulates more easily on sand than on bare ground
- Collapse slopes steeper than 33°
- Finally, round crests slightly and set slip faces to 31-33°. Cache the result.
Footprints and collapse:
- Press down height using shoe sole shape, pile displaced amount on edges (volume conservation)
- Every frame, flow sand to 8 neighbors only if too steep. Stopped sand collapses to 34°, flowing sand collapses to 28°
- Make wet sand harder to collapse

Blowing sand:
- Turn exactly the same volume as eroded into particles, add back to height with integer atomics upon landing (total sand amount remains constant)
- Gravity + air resistance + wind
- Dust has 3 layers (dense core / outer / long-drifting), with self-shadowing and terrain shadowing
Appearance (custom shader):
- Normal = Height + mix two ripples with different wavelengths/directions using noise + pixel-sized grain bumps
- Diffusion uses d'Eon's Lambert-sphere + Hapke
- Shadows receive blue sky light and warm bounce light from surrounding sunlit areas
- Sparkle: Light points <1px fixed in world space only when half-vector between sun and eye is close to ripple normal (creates band of light toward sun)
- Self-shadowing via ray-marching on height field
Lighting and Camera:
- Place low sun (13-16°) on downwind side, separate light/shadow at crests
- Several layers of aerial perspective fog
- Export video at 120fps, average 4 frames with linear light to get 30fps (natural motion blur)

entries.title: Pachinko Animation Prompt
entries.description: A detailed prompt for generating a pachinko-style animation GIF explaining the difference between conversational AI and AI agents, created with Opus 5.5.
entries.prompt:
会話型AI と AIエージェント の違いを、パチンコの激アツリーチ演出で魅せるアニメーションGIFにしてください。内容は薄くてOK、ただし嘘はNG。インパクト最優先、でも文字は読める速さで。

【お題】
「来週、Aさんと30分の会議を入れて」という依頼で対決させる。
会話型AIは調整メールの文面までは完璧に書けるが、送信やカレンダー登録はできない。
AIエージェントはツールを使って、予定確認 → 空き照合 → 承認 → 招待送信まで進めて完了させる。

【演出の流れ】
1. 「ドパ注意」警告（黄黒ストライプ＋赤点滅）→ 左右から迫ってVS着弾
2. ROUND 1：会話型AI
 チャット画面に調整メールがタイピング表示 → 「文面HIT!!」
 → 「送信とカレンダー登録はご自身でお願いします」で縦線ガーン
 → 弱点テロップ「考えて書けるけど、手は動かせない」
3. 保留が青→緑→赤→金に変化 → 擬似連NEXT×3 → リーチ!! → 虹背景で激アツ
 → 役物落下でAIエージェント降臨（カレンダー・メール・検索のツールアイコンが装着される）
4. ROUND 2：AIエージェント
 光の玉がツールをたどってHOPする
 HOP 1：カレンダーで自分の予定を確認
 HOP 2：Aさんの空き枠と照合して候補を決定
 HOP 3：「この内容で送信しますか？」→ 画面中央に「PUSH!!」ボタン演出 → 人が承認
 → 招待送信 →「予定登録 確定!!」で紙吹雪
5. 比較表（できること／動き方／リスク／向いている仕事）
 → AIエージェントにWINスタンプ。ただし「手軽さと安全性は会話型AIに軍配」「相談や壁打ちなら会話型で十分」も入れる
 → 結論「考えるなら会話型、動かすならエージェント。使い分けた人が、勝ち。」

【仕様】
・SVGで1枚ずつフレームを描き、PNG化してGIFに変換
・640×360、12fps、20〜30秒、無限ループ、15MB以内
・日本語は極太ゴシック、金グラデ文字＋黒フチ
・音の代わりに画面揺れ・白フラッシュ・集中線・後光で盛る
・テロップは最低1秒止める
・実在のサービス名やロゴは使わず、汎用アイコンで描く
・書き出し後、主要フレームの一覧画像で文字切れ・重なりを確認して直す
entries.translated_prompt:
Please create an animated GIF showcasing the difference between Conversational AI and AI Agents using a hot Pachinko reach effect. Content can be light, but no lies allowed. Prioritize impact, but keep text readable speed.

[Topic]
Have them compete based on the request: "Schedule a 30-minute meeting with Person A next week."
Conversational AI can perfectly write the adjustment email draft but cannot send it or register it in the calendar.
AI Agents use tools to proceed through schedule confirmation -> availability check -> approval -> invitation sending to completion.

[Direction Flow]
1. "Dopa Warning" (Yellow/Black Stripes + Red Blinking) -> Approaching from left/right to VS Impact
2. ROUND 1: Conversational AI
 Adjustment email typing display on chat screen -> "Draft HIT!!"
 -> "Please handle sending and calendar registration yourself" with vertical line shock
 -> Weakness caption: "Can think and write, but hands don't move"
3. Reserve balls change Blue->Green->Red->Gold -> Pseudo-chain NEXT x3 -> Reach!! -> Hot background with rainbow
 -> Mechanism drop brings AI Agent descent (Calendar, Email, Search tool icons equipped)
4. ROUND 2: AI Agent
 Light ball hops following tools
 HOP 1: Check own schedule on Calendar
 HOP 2: Match with Person A's available slots to decide candidates
 HOP 3: "Send this content?" -> "PUSH!!" button effect in center -> Human approves
 -> Send invitation -> "Registration Confirmed!!" with confetti
5. Comparison Table (What they can do / How they work / Risks / Suitable jobs)
 -> WIN stamp for AI Agent. However, include "Convenience and Safety go to Conversational AI" and "For consultation or brainstorming, Conversational AI is enough"
 -> Conclusion: "Think with Conversational, Act with Agents. Those who use both wisely win."

[Specs]
- Draw frames one by one in SVG, convert to PNG then GIF
- 640x360, 12fps, 20-30 seconds, infinite loop, under 15MB
- Japanese font: Extra Bold Gothic, Gold gradient text with black outline
- Use screen shake, white flash, concentration lines, halo instead of sound

entries.title: Low-Poly Car Animation Storyboard

entries.prompt:
[References]
<Man> corresponds to @Image 2. Use only his appearance: bald round low-poly head, simple dot eyes, short brows, orange t-shirt, seatbelt.
<Woman> corresponds to @Image 1, the passenger on the left. Use only her appearance: shoulder-length wavy brown hair, purple t-shirt, seatbelt.
<Teal Car> corresponds to @Image 1 and @Image 3. Use its body, color and interior.
<Fries Bag> corresponds to @Image 4: a plain brown paper bag with a plain red fries carton full of golden low-poly fries, no printing.
@Image 3 defines the parking-lot location and the exterior shot: the car parked between white lines in front of a beige fast food building with a red awning.
@Image 1 defines only the windshield two-shot framing, the seats and the characters' positions. Do not use its drive-thru menu board or its brick wall: in this video the background through the windows is the parking lot and the beige building from @Image 3.
@Image 2 defines the medium close-up framing of <Man> behind the wheel: his whole head, shoulders, seatbelt and both hands on the steering wheel in frame, with the car roof and windows around him. Do not crop tighter than @Image 2.
@Image 4 defines the close-up framing of <Fries Bag> on <Man>'s lap.
There are exactly two people in the car: <Man> in the driver seat on the right of the windshield shots, <Woman> in the passenger seat on the left. Do not swap their seats.

[Visual Style]
Low-poly faceted 3D toy render exactly like the references: flat soft even daylight, matte materials, saturated warm colors, bright clear blue sky, chunky low-poly trees. Simple stylized animation: small head turns, blinks, brow changes, chewing and hand moves only. No realism, no film grain, no depth-of-field blur. No text, letters, logos, captions or speech bubbles anywhere.

[Shots]
0-3 seconds: Shot 1, the exterior from @Image 3. <Teal Car> sits parked and still. End state: the car is parked, both people visible small through the windshield.
3-5 seconds: Shot 2, hard cut to the windshield two-shot. <Man> holds <Fries Bag> on his lap and opens its top. <Woman>'s hand is already inside the bag. End state: her hand is in the bag, he stares down at it.
5-10 seconds: Shot 3, hard cut to the close-up from @Image 4. <Woman>'s hand pinches fries out of the carton, pulls them out of frame, then comes back for more. End state: her hand is back in the carton.
10-12 seconds: Shot 4, hard cut to the windshield two-shot. <Woman> chews happily with her eyes closed and a big smile, holding fries; her mouth moves as she talks. <Man> stares at her flatly. End state: she is still chewing and smiling.
12-15 seconds: Shot 5, hard cut to the close-up of <Man> from @Image 2, the parking lot behind. Flat deadpan face, mouth closed, eyes slowly narrowing. End state: he looks

entries.prompt: single html file, no libraries. raymarch a watch movement in a webgl2 shader with sdfs: barrel, 4-wheel train with real ratios, escape wheel + pallet fork, balance with hairspring, bridges, rubies. keep it ticking at 4 hz while it explodes layer by layer. hud with live bph.

entries.title: Teardown Skill: Building 3D Machine Simulators with Code
entries.description: Detailed prompts for using the 'teardown' Claude Skill with Opus 5.5 to build interactive 3D simulators of machines from reference images.
entries.prompt:
【我如何把任何机器变成一个可以拆解的 3D 模拟器】

一个免费的 Claude Skill，就能为任何机器构建可运转的 3D 模型，配有实时仪表，每个部件都有对应的按钮。下面是安装配置方法和全部 9 段提示词。

有一个免费的 Claude Skill，可以把任何机器做成 3D 模拟器。你可以环绕观察它、把它剖开，看清正在工作的部件。

这个 Skill 叫 teardown。它免费，在 Claude Code 中运行。

【你要构建的是什么】

一个模拟器就是一个 800 KB 的 HTML 页面，可以离线运行。

【你需要准备什么】

· Claude Code，任何包含它的套餐都可以。我全部使用 Opus 5.5 运行。
· Node.js 20 或更新版本。
· ffmpeg 和 Python 3，只有制作视频和声音时才需要。你可以让 Claude Code 帮你安装这两个工具。

这个 Skill 叫 teardown：MIT 许可证，免费，内含 3 台机器。它基于 whaleyxbt 的 claude-motion 构建，逐帧捕获功能和声音引擎都来自该项目。

【第 1 步：安装 Skill】

npx skills add elvarofficial/teardown -g -a claude-code

然后，在安装目录中执行一次：

cd ~/.claude/skills/teardown && npm install && npx playwright install chromium

打开 Claude Code，输入 /teardown。

【第 2 步：选择机器，寻找参考】

这一步决定了一切。我是吃过亏才明白的。

我曾经在不给任何参考资料的情况下，让它做穿山甲、犰狳和蝎子。三个结果都像普通玩具。后来，我给同一个模型看了一段真实的 V8 模拟器视频，它就把发动机连同各个面板都重建出来了。

所以，选择一台由单一运动输入驱动、且有真实参数的机器，再找一份视觉参考：手册里的剖面图、一张照片，或者一段视频。下面这 5 个我还没有做过：

1. 在 11 片飞轮之间换挡的自行车后拨链器。
2. 以 4 Hz 频率运行的机械表擒纵机构。
3. 汽车转弯时的差速器。
4. 缝出锁式线迹的缝纫机。
5. 挖起一斗土的挖掘机机械臂。

【第 3 步：构建机器】

把下面这段粘贴到 Claude Code 中。替换所有 [方括号] 中的内容。

【提示词 1】
「
/teardown 把 [赛斯纳 337 主起落架] 构建成交互式 3D 模拟器。已附参考：[起落架剖面图]。

使用真实单位，通过代码构建：[主安装板、液压执行器、齿条、输出轴上的小齿轮、万向接头、侧管、弹性支腿和机轮]。

在绘制任何东西之前，先将模型写成一组只依赖单一输入的纯函数：[从 0 到 1 的行程]。使用真实参数：[齿条移动 201 毫米，小齿轮有 32 个齿，模数为 4 毫米，因此支腿恰好转动 180°]。手算核对这些参数，并向我展示核对过程。如果你不确定某个数值是否真实，请明确说明，并告诉我它的来源。

每个部件、每个面板、每个标签，都从这同一个模型读取数据。不要手工为任何部件编排动画。
」

为什么这套方法行得通：

· 模型先行。起落架、仪表和时间线读取同一个函数，因此不会彼此脱节。
· 一个输入。用一个数值决定整套机构的姿态，才是一套机构。手工给 12 个零件分别编排动画，得到的只是 12 段动画。

【第 4 步：构建控制台】

【提示词 2】
「
以 1600×900 的布局，在机器周围布置控制台：
· 左上角放标题和最主要的实时数值，字号要大：[发动机转速，单位 rpm]
· 随机器运动同步变化的实时图表：[曲轴转过 720° 期间的气门升程、当前跟踪气缸的压力—容积循环曲线]
· 一个原理图面板，基于同一个模型，以 2D 方式重绘机构
· 每个子系统对应一个按钮：将其隔离、剖切、单独展示
· 用按钮切换相机视角：[主展示视角、正面、侧面、顶部、V 形气缸夹角内部]
· 用细引线将标注连接到对应的零件
每个面板都根据当前帧的状态重新绘制。屏幕上的数值都不是手工填入的。
」

【第 5 步：确定视觉风格】

【提示词 3】
「
风格：浅色摄影棚中的干净研究模型。
· 浅色背景，不可见的地面上投下柔和阴影，只用一种强调色，标出当前正在工作的部件
· 机器占其视窗的 60% 到 70%
· 深色部件带光泽，缸套采用玻璃材质，金属粗糙度至少为 0.45，避免出现白色条状高光
· 如果某个部件接近白色，就给它加一圈细墨线轮廓，或者使用更深色的地面
· 根据机构选择机位：如果正面看起来挤成一片网格，就使用 3/4 侧视角
」

【第 6 步：像挑剔的评论者一样检查】

【提示词 4】
「
在向我展示任何东西之前：
1. 在自动导览的每个关键节点渲染一张静帧，逐张检查：有没有部件穿过其他部件，有没有部件脱离安装位置悬空，有没有标签遮住它标注的对象，有没有数值与当前姿态不符。
2. 以 0.2 秒为间隔逐步检查每一段过渡，寻找突跳。
3. 通过修改参数区里的数值修正碰撞。绝不要靠相机角度把问题藏起来。
告诉我你检查了什么，修正了什么。把静帧展示给我。
」

【第 7 步：做成一个由你操控的页面】

【提示词 5】
「
把模拟器做成一个可以由用户操控的页面：
· 自动播放视频里的导览流程，用一个光标移动到各个按钮并点击
· 任何点击、拖拽、滚动或按键，都会把控制权交给访客；25 秒没有操作，就交回自动导览
· 拖拽环绕观察，滚动缩放，用一个按键隐藏面板
· 在第一帧之前预热所有着色器，避免页面卡住
· 在集成显卡上测试，并增加画质档位：关闭环境光遮蔽、降低像素比、降低阴影分辨率、面板每隔一帧重绘一次
」

【第 8 步：把它做成视频】

录制：

【提示词 6】
「
录制自动导览：render(t) 必须是时间的纯函数，因此请在无头 Chrome 中，以 60 fps、1920×1080 的规格逐帧绘制，并通过管道传给 ffmpeg，使用 H.264、yuv420p 和 faststart。然后向我展示一张包含所有关键节点的静帧拼接预览图。
」

配乐与音效：

【提示词 7】
「
在同一条时间线上，用代码编配音乐与音效：[92 bpm 的 Am9 和弦，每个做功冲程配一声柔和的低沉敲击，让油门加大时节奏随之变密；每次按下按钮时配一声轻微的点击；拖动油门时，底下铺逐渐增强的气流声]。将母带处理至 -14 LUFS，真峰值低于 -1 dB，然后将音轨封装进视频。
」

当 GPU 负载很高时，录屏工具会丢帧。按时间定位、逐帧渲染的导览不会有这个问题。

【第 9 步：发布到网上】

【提示词 8】
「
把模拟器发布为网页：
· 将 HTML 控制在 1 MB 以内；把任何大型模型移出去，作为独立文件与页面放在一起
· 从最佳画面制作一张 1200×630 的预览卡片，图片使用绝对 URL
· 部署到 Vercel
」

1 MB 这条要求，来自我踩过的一次坑。我的兔子页面把模型嵌在内部，体积达到 15.9 MB，X 始终不显示链接预览卡片。把模型移出去后，页面变成 967 KB，卡片就出现了。

【额外玩法：让他们把机器推到极限】

【提示词 9】
「
添加一个滑块，用于控制 [风速，0 到 15 m/s]，拖动时实时运行模型：[微风只能让曲柄缓慢转动，强风则让机械腿快到模糊]。在同一组面板中展示这些变化。
」
entries.translated_prompt:
[How I Turn Any Machine Into a Disassemblable 3D Simulator]

A free Claude Skill can build operable 3D models for any machine, complete with real-time gauges and buttons for every component. Below are the installation configuration steps and all 9 prompts.

There is a free Claude Skill that turns any machine into a 3D simulator. You can orbit around it, cut it open, and see the parts working.

This Skill is called teardown. It is free and runs in Claude Code.

[What You Are Building]

A simulator is an 800 KB HTML page that runs offline.

[What You Need to Prepare]

· Claude Code, any plan that includes it works. I run everything on Opus 5.5.
· Node.js 20 or newer.
· ffmpeg and Python 3, only needed if making videos and sounds. You can have Claude Code help you install these two tools.

The Skill is called teardown: MIT license, free, comes with 3 machines. It is built based on whaleyxbt's claude-motion; the frame-by-frame capture feature and sound engine come from that project.

[Step 1: Install the Skill]

npx skills add elvarofficial/teardown -g -a claude-code

Then, run once in the installation directory:

cd ~/.claude/skills/teardown && npm install && npx playwright install chromium

Open Claude Code and type /teardown.

[Step 2: Choose a Machine, Find References]

This step determines everything. I learned this the hard way.

I used to ask it to make pangolins, armadillos, and scorpions without giving any reference materials. All three results looked like ordinary toys. Later, when I showed the same model a real V8 simulator video, it rebuilt the engine along with all its panels.

So, choose a machine driven by a single motion input with real parameters, and find a visual reference: a cross-section diagram from a manual, a photo, or a video. Here are 5 I haven't done yet:

1. A bicycle rear derailleur shifting between 11 sprockets.
2. A mechanical watch escapement running at 4 Hz.
3. A car differential during turning.
4. A sewing machine creating a lockstitch.
5. An excavator arm digging up a bucket of soil.

[Step 3: Build the Machine]

Paste the following into Claude Code. Replace all content in [square brackets].

[Prompt 1]
«
/teardown Build [Cessna 337 main landing gear] as an interactive 3D simulator. Reference attached: [landing gear cross-section diagram].

Use real units, build via code: [main mounting plate, hydraulic actuator, rack, pinion on output shaft, universal joint, side tubes, elastic legs, and wheels].

Before drawing anything, write the model as a set of pure functions depending on a single input: [stroke from 0 to 1]. Use real parameters: [rack moves 201 mm, pinion has 32 teeth, module is 4 mm, so the leg rotates exactly 180°]. Verify these parameters by hand calculation and show me the verification process. If you are unsure whether a value is real, state it clearly and tell me its source.

Every part, every panel, every label reads data from this same model. Do not manually animate any parts.
»

Why this method works:

· Model first. The landing gear, gauges, and timeline read the same function, so they won't be out of sync.
· One input. Using one number to determine the pose of the entire mechanism makes it a mechanism. Manually animating 12 parts separately just gives you 12 animations.

[Step 4: Build the Console]

[Prompt 2]
«
Layout the console around the machine in a 1600×900 layout:
· Top-left corner: Title and most important real-time values, large font size: [Engine RPM, unit rpm]
· Real-time charts synchronized with machine movement: [Valve lift during crankshaft rotation of 720°, Pressure-Volume loop curve for the currently tracked cylinder]
· A schematic panel, redrawing the mechanism in 2D based on the same model
· One button per subsystem: isolate, cut away, display separately
· Buttons to switch camera views: [Main showcase view, Front, Side, Top, Inside the V-cylinder angle]
· Connect labels to corresponding parts with thin leader lines
Every panel is redrawn based on the current frame's state. No numbers on screen are manually entered.
»

[Step 5: Determine Visual Style]

[Prompt 3]
«
Style: Clean research model in a light studio.
· Light background, soft shadows cast on an invisible ground plane, use only one accent color to highlight the part currently working
· Machine occupies 60% to 70% of its viewport
· Dark parts have gloss, cylinder liners use glass material, metal roughness at least 0.45 to avoid white strip highlights
· If a part is nearly white, add a thin ink outline or use a darker ground plane
· Choose camera position based on the mechanism: if the front view looks crowded like a grid, use a 3/4 side view
»

[Step 6: Check Like a Picky Critic]

[Prompt 4]
«
Before showing me anything:
1. Render a still frame at each key node of the auto-tour, check them one by one: Are parts intersecting other parts? Are parts floating detached from their mounting positions? Are labels obscuring the objects they annotate? Do values mismatch the current pose?
2. Check every transition segment by segment at 0.2-second intervals, looking for jumps.
3. Fix collisions by modifying values in the parameter area. Never hide problems with camera angles.
Tell me what you checked and what you fixed. Show me the still frames.
»

[Step 7: Make It a User-Controlled Page]

[Prompt 5]
«
Turn the simulator into a user-controllable page:
· Auto-play the tour flow from the video, using a cursor to move to buttons and click them
· Any click, drag, scroll, or key press hands control over to the visitor; after 25 seconds of no action, return to auto-tour
· Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, use a key to hide panels
· Pre-warm all shaders before the first frame to prevent page freezing
· Test on integrated graphics and add quality tiers: disable ambient occlusion, lower pixel ratio, lower shadow resolution, redraw panels every other frame
»

[Step 8: Make It a Video]

Recording:

[Prompt 6]
«
Record the auto-tour: render(t) must be a pure function of time, so please draw frame-by-frame in headless Chrome at 60 fps, 1920×1080 specification, pipe through ffmpeg using H.264, yuv420p, and faststart. Then show me a stitched preview image containing all key nodes.
»

Music and Sound Effects:

[Prompt 7]
«
Compose music and sound effects via code on the same timeline: [Am9 chord at 92 bpm, a soft low thud for each power stroke, rhythm becomes denser as throttle increases; a slight click for each button press; a gradually increasing airflow sound under the track when dragging the throttle]. Master to -14 LUFS, true peak below -1 dB, then encapsulate the audio track into the video.
»

When GPU load is high, screen recording tools drop frames. Time-positioned, frame-by-frame rendered tours do not have this problem.

[Step 9: Publish Online]

[Prompt 8]
«
Publish the simulator as a web page:
· Keep HTML under 1 MB; move any large models out as separate files alongside the page
· Create a 1200×630 preview card from the best shot, images use absolute URLs
· Deploy to Vercel
»

The 1 MB requirement comes from a pitfall I encountered. My rabbit page embedded the model internally, reaching 15.9 MB, and X never displayed the link preview card. After moving the model out, the page became 967 KB, and the card appeared.

[Bonus: Let Them Push the Machine to the Limit]

[Prompt 9]
«
Add a slider to control [Wind speed, 0 to 15 m/s], run the model in real-time while dragging: [Light breeze only slowly turns the crank, strong wind makes the mechanical legs move so fast they blur]. Display these changes in the same set of panels.
»

entries.title: Kinetic Typography Video with Opus
entries.description: Guide to creating a 30-second kinetic typography video using only code and Opus 5.5, detailing font changes, camera angles, and animation techniques.
entries.prompt: Create a 30-second kinetic typography video where each line changes font, color, movement, and camera angle. Use no external media; generate everything via code. Techniques: change fonts per word for expression, make text react to sound by bouncing, lay text flat as background, create 3D corridors for camera passage, switch colors/fonts rhythmically, flow liquid patterns inside text, rotate text rings while swapping central words, end with whitespace and cursor. Specify direction in words like 'make text the floor' or 'pass through text'. Define changing elements (font, color, layout, camera) per line. Place text in 3D space for depth. Check frames as images to fix overlaps.

entries.title: Lo-fi Pixel Art City Loop Prompt
entries.description: Detailed prompt for generating a 10-hour lo-fi pixel art animation of a rainy futuristic city corner in HTML Canvas/WebGL.
entries.prompt: 构建自包含HTML5 Canvas（或WebGL）像素艺术动画，作为10小时循环lo-fi音乐视频背景。场景设定为2089年凌晨2:37的雨夜未来都市角落，连续降雨，街道湿透，氛围忧郁、温馨且神秘，科技主导下仍有人性温暖。构图分层并注重叙事：前景屋顶小屋或公寓（温暖室内、剪影与小物件）、中景建筑群含空调、电线、自动售货机与全息招牌、远景天际线与高架列车/飞行器。色彩以深蓝、青绿、靛蓝冷调为主，暖琥珀色窗户与灯火、品红/紫罗兰霓虹形成强对比，湿面反射清晰，整体暗调但不泥泞。动画要求多层独立循环、无跳变：多速多深度雨（含斜风）、漂移雾霾、上升烟雾、滴水与涟漪、不规则闪烁霓虹与指示灯、屏幕内容循环、室内灯光波动、偶尔火花、旋转风扇、远处车辆与窗户内活动、轻微摇摆元素，整体催眠放松。严格真实像素风格，内部分辨率640×360，整数3倍最近邻放大，所有效果遵守像素网格。直接输出完整可运行的单文件代码，支持流畅60fps、长时稳定、固定镜头、正确缩放与全屏无UI模式。
entries.translated_prompt: Build a self-contained HTML5 Canvas (or WebGL) pixel art animation serving as a background for a 10-hour looped lo-fi music video. The scene is set in a rainy corner of a futuristic city at 2:37 AM in 2089, with continuous rain, wet streets, and an atmosphere that is melancholic, warm, and mysterious, retaining human warmth despite technology dominance. Use layered composition with narrative focus: foreground features a rooftop hut or apartment (warm interior, silhouettes, small objects); midground includes buildings with AC units, wires, vending machines, and holographic signs; background shows the skyline and elevated trains/flying vehicles. Color palette dominated by deep blue, teal, and indigo cool tones, contrasted strongly with warm amber windows/lights and magenta/violet neon. Wet reflections should be clear; overall dark but not muddy. Animation requires multiple independent loops without jumps: multi-speed/multi-depth rain (including wind drift), drifting fog, rising smoke, dripping water and ripples, irregularly flickering neon and indicator lights, looping screen content, fluctuating indoor lights, occasional sparks, rotating fans, distant vehicle activity and window movements, slight swaying elements, all hypnotic and relaxing. Strict authentic pixel art style, internal resolution 640x360, integer 3x nearest-neighbor scaling, all effects adhere to the pixel grid. Output complete runnable single-file code directly, supporting smooth 60fps, long-term stability, fixed camera, correct scaling, and fullscreen UI-less mode.

entries.title: Sound Journey 3D Animation
entries.description: Creating a 3D animation visualizing sound traveling from air to brain using Three.js and Opus 5.5.
entries.prompt: Create a video showing the journey of one sound from air to brain without video generation tools. Path: Air -> Eardrum -> Ossicles -> Cochlea -> Fluid Wave -> Hair Cells -> Auditory Nerve -> Brain. Extend base playing with Suno MCP. Analyze beats. Use Three.js to 3D model ear to brain. Sync camera, waves, and text to beats. Export with HyperFrames.

entries.title: Sound Synced 3D Bass Guitar Animation
entries.description: Workflow description for creating a video showing sound traveling through a 3D bass guitar model, synced to audio beats using Claude Code (Opus 5.5).
entries.prompt:
実物写真からコードで3Dにした自分のベースで、1音の旅を見せる動画、動画生成なし
弦 → 磁石 → コイル → 銅線 → 増幅 → スピーカー → 空気
音は自分の曲をSuno MCPでカバー。その曲を測って、映像を全部合わせた
主打点52か所で、98%が1コマ以内のズレ

──────────────
制作フロー
Claude Code(Opus 5.5)が司令塔 / 実物写真 → Three.jsで3Dベース → Suno MCPで曲のカバー → 打点を解析 → カメラ・稲妻・文字を打点に同期 → HyperFramesで書き出し
──────────────
entries.translated_prompt:
Show the journey of a single note through a 3D bass guitar modeled from a real photo using code, without video generation.
String -> Magnet -> Coil -> Copper Wire -> Amplification -> Speaker -> Air
Cover your own song with Suno MCP. Measure the track and align all visuals.
At 52 main beat points, 98% are within 1 frame of deviation.

──────────────
Production Flow
Claude Code (Opus 5.5) as commander / Real photo -> 3D base with Three.js -> Cover song with Suno MCP -> Analyze beats -> Sync camera, lightning, and text to beats -> Export with HyperFrames

entries.title: Halloween Code Animation
entries.description: A comprehensive prompt for generating a 17-second vertical Halloween animation with synchronized sound effects created entirely through code (HTML Canvas, Python/Numpy, FFmpeg), avoiding AI video/image models.
entries.prompt:
Make a 17-second vertical (1080x1920, 30 fps) Halloween animation with sound, using only code. No video model, no image model, no audio samples.
Draw every pixel on an HTML canvas, synthesize every sound in Python (numpy), render frame by frame with a headless browser, mux with ffmpeg at -14 LUFS.
Core rule: every sound must be caused by something you can see.
- A ghost hops from pumpkin to pumpkin. Each landing lights that pumpkin's face and plays its note. 9 pumpkins = 9 pitches like a keyboard: 7 orange in front (A3 B3 C4 D4 E4 G4 A4), 2 white behind (Bb3, D#4). Note names under each pumpkin.
- From ~3 s: three tombstones jump on every beat = bass.
- From ~6 s: the moon pulses = kick; bats beat their wings = hi-hat.
- Chorus: lightning = clap; 8 more ghosts burst out of the graves and land on the chord's pumpkins = organ chord stabs.
Music: Grieg, "In the Hall of the Mountain King" (1875, public domain), A minor. Play the 4-bar theme twice as one accelerando (eighth note 0.22 s -> 0.12 s), then a snare roll + riser,
then 0.75 s of near silence (screen goes dark, the ghost hangs mid-air, caption "WAIT…"). Chorus at ~2/3 of the video: flash, crash, full organ chord, pumpkins catch fire. End on one big A-minor hit with all 9 ghosts landing at once.
Loop it: after the final hit the other ghosts fly off and the first ghost jumps back onto pumpkin A, landing exactly on frame 0.
Captions (top third): first frame "A GHOST PLAYS / THE PUMPKINS / Claude Opus 5.5 wrote every frame and every note" with sound at 0.0 s; then "THE GRAVES ARE THE BASS", "BATS = HI-HAT / MOON = KICK", "WAIT…", "EVERYBODY OUT!", "HAPPY HALLOWEEN / name the song?".
Compute all events in Python first, save them to JSON, and make the canvas a pure function renderAt(t) of that JSON, so picture and sound can never drift apart.

entries.title: Opus 5.5 Blender 3D Animation Workflow

entries.prompt:
Step 1: Install Blender 5.2.2 and the official Blender MCP server.
Step 2: Open Claude, pick Opus 5.5 on high effort and run /mcp to confirm Blender is connected.
Step 3: Install BlenderKit (Edit > Preferences > Install from Disk) for 140K+ free models, materials and HDRIs.
Step 4: Ask Opus "can you see the BlenderKit library?", so it runs a test search before you build anything.
Step 5: Paste a reference image and a plain prompt. Talk to it like a junior 3D designer, no structured prompts.
Step 6: For characters, ask for the rig in the same prompt ("keep it realistic, rig it for smooth animation").
Step 7: Render a 480p preview first, then the final render (1080p can take 1-2 hours).

Rule: Never let Opus build a chair from scratch. It burns tokens and still looks fake. Pull the asset and let Opus arrange it.
Check the animation step by step before the final render.

pick the zoom's fixed point so the video frame

entries.title: Marimba Physics Animation Prompt
entries.description: A detailed prompt for Claude Opus 5.5 to create a Blender animation featuring marimba music synthesized via Python and rigid body physics for balls hitting plates, rendered as MP4.
entries.prompt:
曲と音

曲は【曲名】。著作権が切れている曲か、自分の曲を使う。楽譜（音の高さと長さ）は信頼できる出典から取って、出典を教えて。
音はマリンバだけで、Python で一から合成する（録音や音源素材は使わない）。メロディに、低音の伴奏をマリンバで付ける。長い音はロール（トレモロ）にする。

物理

ボールは Blender の剛体物理で落とす。次の音の時刻にボールがいる場所へ次の板を置き、板の傾きと反発係数を逆算して、当たる時刻のずれを1ミリ秒未満にそろえる。
最後に通しで計算し直して、当たりが音の数と同じか（余計な当たりがないか）確かめる。
最後の音のあとにボールが板から落ちていかないよう、受け止めるもの（お椀など）を置く。

見た目

場面は【例：夕暮れの里山。手まり柄のボール、木のマリンバの板】。板は当たった瞬間に光って、波紋が出る。
カメラはボールを追いかけ、最後は引きの全景にする。地形や建物がボールやカメラの視線をふさがないようにする。
本番の前に見本のコマを数枚見せて。本番の描画は、所要時間を伝えて了承を取ってから、休憩を入れながら回して。

仕上げ

縦 1080×1920 の MP4。右下に【自分のロゴ】。
左に Blender の作業画面風（ソリッド表示＋ポリゴンの辺の線）、右に完成版を並べた横長 1920×1080 の比較動画も作る。左右の見出しは「Blender 物理演算プレビュー」と「完成（レンダー）」。
entries.translated_prompt:
Music and Sound

The song is {argument name="song name" default="[Song Name]"}. Use a public domain song or your own composition. Obtain sheet music (pitch and duration) from a reliable source and cite it.
Synthesize sound from scratch using Python with only a marimba (do not use recordings or audio assets). Add bass accompaniment with marimba to the melody. Long notes should be rolls (tremolo).

Physics

Drop balls using Blender's rigid body physics. Place the next plate where the ball will be at the time of the next note, calculating the plate's angle and coefficient of restitution to align the impact timing error to less than 1 millisecond.
Recalculate everything at the end to ensure the number of impacts matches the number of notes (no extra impacts).
Place a catcher (like a bowl) so the ball does not fall off the plate after the last note.

Visuals

Scene: {argument name="scene description" default="Twilight rural landscape. Temari-patterned ball, wooden marimba plates"}. Plates glow and ripple upon impact.
Camera follows the ball, ending with a wide shot. Ensure terrain or buildings do not obstruct the ball or camera view.
Show sample frames before final render. For the final render, ask for approval after estimating time, rendering in chunks with breaks.

Output

Vertical 1080x1920 MP4. Logo in bottom right: {argument name="logo" default="[Your Logo]"}.
Also create a horizontal 1920x1080 comparison video: Left side shows Blender viewport style (solid display + polygon edges), Right side shows the final render. Labels: "Blender Physics Preview" and "Final Render".

entries.title: Rewindable Particle Video
entries.description: A prompt to create a React/Remotion video where an interface explodes into particles that can be rewound precisely by scrubbing the timeline, ensuring no drift or glitches.
entries.prompt:
I always wondered why AI videos fall apart the moment you try to change anything, so I asked Opus 5.5 to build one where time itself is just a slider I can grab

> one click and the whole interface explodes into thousands of glowing particles
> drag the timeline back and every single one flies home to the exact pixel it came from
> scrub it forward, backward, jerk it around as fast as you want, and it never drifts or glitches
> no After Effects and no hand-placed keyframes, the entire thing is React code rendered with Remotion

The trick is surprisingly simple: nothing in the video remembers what happened before, every frame is calculated from the current time alone, so playing it backwards is exactly as precise as playing it forward

entries.title: Kurzgesagt Style Animated Explainer Prompt
entries.description: A comprehensive prompt for Claude Opus 5.5 to generate code-based animated explainer videos in the style of Kurzgesagt, featuring specific visual directions, scene structures, and rendering instructions.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: one topic as a "what if" question (default: "{argument name="topic" default="What if the Sun vanished?"}"), the length (default {argument name="length" default="30 seconds"}), and whether I have an ElevenLabs key (if not, use a free local voice).
</inputs>

<direction>
A Kurzgesagt-style animated explainer at 1920x1080, 30fps, drawn entirely in code: one 2D canvas plus one WebGL canvas for planets.
Space: a vertical gradient #081d2c to #102348, five huge parallax nebula blobs (teal rgb 24,150,160 at 20%, blue 40,95,195 at 16%, coral 220,95,110 at 10%, indigo 60,70,175 at 15%), three star layers at parallax depths .12/.35/.6 that twinkle, 40% of the near stars drawn as 4-point sparkles.
The Sun: radius 300px, half off the left edge. A radial gradient #fff7dc to #ffc857 to #ff8f4a with an offset highlight, additive halo rings at 1.23/1.48/1.76/2.1x the radius, 18 faint rotating ray wedges, 28 drifting glowing granules on its surface.
Earth: an orthographic sphere in a fragment shader, 4x supersampled, from a 2048x1024 map painted from longitude/latitude polygons: land #5fc47a, forest #48ad6b, desert #f5c75f, rainforest #3a9d62, ice #f1f8ff, ocean gradient #4dc7eb to #1a66b8, white capsule clouds. Tilt .26 rad, spin .55 degrees per second. Day/night uses smoothstep(-.12, .24, N·L) with the light direction recomputed from Sun to Earth every frame. Navy night side with ~380 warm city lights, a coral band on the terminator, a cyan rim, ocean specular, an atmosphere halo that is stronger on the lit side.
A small astronaut mascot (~180px) built from rounded rectangles: suit #f3f7fb, orange #ff8f4a boots, a visor gradient #1f5a73 to #0a1c2c with glowing cyan eyes that look at whatever matters, a blinking antenna light, an idle bob, squash and stretch on every pose.
Type: Fredoka 600/700 only. Captions in caps with 3-6px letter spacing in teal #8fd8e6, gold #ffd98a or white, sitting in rounded pills of rgb(6,20,40) at 62%. Every line of text rises 1.3x its own height through a clip on an ease-out-quint.
Finish: a vignette to rgba(4,4,20,.45) and a 6% film grain re-randomized 24 times per second.
Banned: outlines, flares or loops on the Sun's edge, static infographic strips, full stops in on-screen text, text that fades in whole, AI images or AI video, Kurzgesagt's own characters, bird or music.
</direction>

<structure>
30 seconds, every line of narration gets a camera move or a transformation, nothing ever holds still.
Tight on the Sun at 2.25x (0s) → on the word "vanished" it swells 6% for 0.22s, collapses in 0.33s, then a white flash and a shockwave ring (1s) → pull back to 1x revealing Earth still lit and the astronaut staring at the empty spot (1.6-3s) → on "eight" an 8:20 countdown slams in from 1.7x to 1x and starts ticking, a "LAST LIGHT" label rides the edge of the growing dark disc (3.2s) → dive to 2.3x on Earth with light streaks flowing in (5.6s) → on "you" a YOU pin drops (7s) → on "left" a photon lands on the pin with "THIS LIGHT LEFT THE SUN / 8 MIN 20 SEC AGO" (7.5s) → on "play" the pin morphs into a play button, "YOU PRESSED PLAY / 15 SEC AGO" (8.8s) → one pull-back from 2.4x to a 0.3x orbit view, "LAST LIGHT" and "GRAVITY" riding the ring (9.6-12.5s) → on "nothing" a dotted circle at the empty centre (13.4s) → on "hits" the darkness sweeps Earth in 0.7s, city lights pop on, the countdown turns gold at 0:00 (15.8s) → on "black" the background fades almost to black (17.4s) → Jupiter appears, "STILL SHINING FOR 1 HOUR+" (17.9s) → zoom out, a dashed tangent line, "30 KM/S" as Earth flies straight off (20.8s) → a thermometer counts 15 to -70°C while frost grows from the poles (22.8s) → a 0.8s rewind on a separate story clock (24.3s) → sunglasses drop onto the astronaut (25.2s) → a photon tagged "8:20 OLD", then the title (27.7s).
For any other topic, keep the same shape: the event happens on its word, pull back to show scale, dive in to make it personal ("you"), pull back out, the consequence with a live counter, an escalation, a funny beat with the mascot, a callback and the title.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file. Every frame is a pure function of time: https://t.co/lT4Z2IvSIB(t) draws frame t. No timers, no CSS animation.
2. Camera moves on easeInOutCubic, zoom is interpolated in log space, every pop is a damped spring (damping .42-.5, frequency 12-16).
3. Voice: ElevenLabs eleven_v4 with a designed voice (calm, warm, curious male, late 30s, crisp, light neutral European English), stability .5, similarity .75, generated with timestamps. Without a key, use kokoro-onnx locally and get word times with faster-whisper. Every animation event fires on its word. About 165 words per minute, 0.24s between sentences, a 0.36s beat before the big reveal.
4. The darkness front: any pixel within the front's radius from the Sun turns to night with a 30px soft edge. The front moves at ~47px/s and ramps to 700px/s near Earth.
5. Keep two clocks: ambient time for twinkle, spin and bob, and a separate story clock for events, so a rewind stays consistent.
6. Render with Playwright in headless Edge with the GPU: seek every frame at 30fps and blend 2 subframes (shutter 0.6) for motion blur, then encode with libx264 at CRF 16 for the master and CRF 20 for delivery.
7. Sound: a calm royalty-free space music bed 7dB under the voice, timed so its natural ending lands on the title, swelling 5dB under the title. One downloaded royalty-free sound effect per event kind (collapse, impact, pull-back whoosh, countdown tick, dive, pin tap, photon land, play click, light hit, reveal, frost, rewind), each peak-aligned to its frame and 4-10dB under the voice. Master with gain plus a limiter to -14 LUFS, -2.2dB true peak.
</build>

<gotchas>
Make the WebGL globe canvas at least 2 x radius x zoom x 1.18 pixels or the sphere clips flat in close-ups. Never draw prominences on the Sun's edge, they read as white hooks. Never pad the voice to fit the visuals, tighten the read instead. Speed the darkness front up near Earth or it takes 13 seconds to cross the planet. Show me a contact sheet of every beat before rendering.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me the inputs, write the narration with the beat each word triggers, show it to me, then build and render the video.
</start>

entries.title: Precise Motion Design with Opus 5.5
entries.description: A 5-step guide to controlling timing and frame rates for motion design using Claude Opus 5.5 and Remotion skills.
entries.prompt:
ترکیب Claude Opus 5.5 و Remotion این امکان رو می‌ده که با ویدیو مثل کد رفتار کنی؛ یعنی زمان‌بندی دقیق داشته باشی و تغییرات رو بدون به‌هم‌ریختن کل انیمیشن اعمال کنی. 🎬

بخش زیادی از مشکلات ساخت ویدیو با AI از اینجا میاد که همه‌چیز رو با پرامپت توصیف می‌کنیم و امیدواریم خروجی درست از آب دربیاد.

اما برای ساخت موشن دقیق، باید زمان‌بندی رو عددی و مشخص تعریف کرد.

این ۵ مرحله رو دنبال کن:

۱. اول مدت ویدیو و فریم‌ریت رو مشخص کن

مثلاً ویدیوی ۲۰ ثانیه‌ای با نرخ ۳۰ فریم بر ثانیه، دقیقاً ۶۰۰ فریم داره.

۲. قبل از نوشتن انیمیشن، اتفاقات اصلی رو مشخص کن

ورود عنصر -» اجرای حرکت -» نمایش نتیجه -» مکث برای خواندن -» پایان

۳. زمان دقیق هر اتفاق رو به Claude بده

مثلاً:

- ظاهر شدن دکمه تا فریم ۹۰
- اجرای کلیک در فریم ۱۹۵
- نمایش خوانای نتیجه از فریم ۲۳۴

به‌جای اینکه بگی «دکمه کمی دیرتر ظاهر بشه»، دقیق مشخص کن چه زمانی باید ظاهر بشه.

۴. اسکیل‌های رسمی Remotion رو نصب کن

برای اینکه Claude با الگوها و روش‌های درست Remotion کار کنه، از اسکیل‌های رسمی این پروژه استفاده کن:

"npx skills add remotion-dev/skills"

۵. قبل از دیدن کل ویدیو، فریم‌های ثابت رو بررسی کن

با بررسی فریم‌های کلیدی می‌تونی ایرادهای چیدمان، زمان‌بندی و خوانایی رو زودتر پیدا کنی و اصلاحات دقیق‌تری انجام بدی.

چرخه کاری پیشنهادی:

فریم‌ها ← بریف ← تولید انیمیشن ← بررسی فریم‌های ثابت ← اصلاح دقیق ← رندر نهایی

💡 نکته اصلی اینه که وقتی زمان‌بندی به‌جای حدس و توصیف مبهم، با اعداد و فریم‌های مشخص کنترل بشه، می‌تونی یک بخش از موشن رو تغییر بدی، بدون اینکه مجبور بشی کل ترکیب‌بندی رو از نو بسازی.

این همون تغییریه که ساخت موشن با Claude رو از آزمون‌وخطای پرامپتی به یک فرایند قابل‌کنترل‌تر تبدیل می‌کنه.

🔗 اسکیل‌های Remotion:
https://t.co/o5LNe2IluB
entries.translated_prompt:
Combining Claude Opus 5.5 and Remotion allows you to treat video like code; meaning you have precise timing and can apply changes without disrupting the entire animation. 🎬

Many problems with AI video creation come from describing everything with a prompt and hoping for the right output.

But for precise motion, timing must be defined numerically and specifically.

Follow these 5 steps:

1. First, specify the video duration and frame rate.
For example, a 20-second video at 30 frames per second has exactly 600 frames.

2. Before writing the animation, define the main events.
Element entry -> Motion execution -> Result display -> Pause for reading -> End

3. Give Claude the exact time for each event.
For example:
- Button appears by frame 90
- Click executes at frame 195
- Clear result display starts from frame 234
Instead of saying "the button should appear a bit later," specify exactly when it should appear.

4. Install official Remotion skills.
To ensure Claude works with correct Remotion patterns and methods, use the project's official skills:
"npx skills add remotion-dev/skills"

5. Check static frames before viewing the whole video.
By checking key frames, you can find layout, timing, and readability issues earlier and make more precise corrections.

Suggested work cycle:
Frames <- Brief <- Animation Generation <- Static Frame Check <- Precise Correction <- Final Render

💡 The main point is that when timing is controlled with specific numbers and frames instead of guesses and vague descriptions, you can change one part of the motion without having to rebuild the entire composition.
This is the change that turns motion creation with Claude from prompt-based trial-and-error into a more controllable process.

🔗 Remotion Skills:
https://t.co/o5LNe2IluB
