entries.title: UI Motion Loop Design Prompt
entries.description: Detailed prompt for creating a 14-second seamless UI motion loop with specific timing, physics, and rendering instructions.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Give me:

* canvas color
* shape color
* accent color
* shape radius
* fonts
* the states the shape should morph through

Use hex codes, seconds, damping ratios and pixel sizes instead of adjectives.
</inputs>

<direction>
Make a 14 second, 1440x1440, 60fps seamless UI motion loop.

One shape, zero cuts.

The shape morphs from state to state and is never replaced.

Each state fills 50% of the frame.

The camera starts on the beat and settles slower than the shape.

Use closed-form springs.

Shape damping 0.72, settle time 0.35s.
Camera damping 1.0, settle time 0.6s.

Content swaps use 12px blur and fade over 0.15s.

The cursor tip stays locked to whatever it drags.
</direction>

<structure>
Use a 0.5s beat grid.

0.0 - pixel mascot idles
1.0 - mascot squashes into play button
1.5 - loader
2.0 - check draws
2.5 - timeline scrub
4.0 - keyframe stretches past the end and snaps back
5.0 - bezier editor
7.0 - counter rolls F 000 to F 840
8.5 - render bar fills
10.0 - command palette types "export mp4"
11.0 - toast says "840 frames rendered"
12.0 - toast shrinks back into the mascot

The last frame must be the first frame.
</structure>

<build>
Write one HTML file with Canvas 2D.

window.renderAt(t) must be a pure function of time.

No Math.random.
No clock.
No carried state.

?t= must freeze the exact moment.

Render every frame from renderAt(frame / 60).

Use 4 subframes for motion blur.

Encode to H.264 at 60fps.
</build>

<gotchas>
Fix the cursor jump at the loop wrap with:

t - 14*floor(t/14)

Do not cross-fade orange into ink.

Use a ripple from the center at 1.5s and from the click point at 12.0s.

Roll word swaps vertically.

Start draw-on after blur-in.

Aim the cursor at where the target will be when it lands.

Keep cursor speed under 65 px/frame.
</gotchas>

<start>
First show me the storyboard.

Then write the code.

After the first render, check 5 frames around every beat and fix the issues before the final render.
</start>

entries.title: Food Craving Product Launch Film
entries.description: Prompt for creating a 15-second product launch film for a food ordering app, detailing scenes, timing, and visual style.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product, the exact request a user types into it, 6 to 8 photos for the result cards, a royalty-free song around 130 BPM with a clear drop (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and my brand mark for the end card. If I skip anything, use the defaults: the food-ordering story below, food photos from Pexels (fire noodles, birria tacos, hot chicken, buffalo wings, smash burger, spicy ramen), and Mixkit "Cat Walk".
</inputs>

<direction>
A 15-second product launch film, 1920x1080 at 60fps. 2D only, one continuous take. No fades, blurs or cuts: each scene grows from the last. Text rises from a mask line, buttons expand into pages, and color floods from one object before shrinking into another. Give the camera one eased move per scene, and never zoom in and out consecutively.

Look: warm white canvas (#f5f5f2), black UI (#0e0e10), lime accent (#cdf24f), orange (#ff6a2a), and a blue send button (#2f6bff). Add an Apple Intelligence-style iridescent glow around the input: a blurred conic gradient rotating through pink, orange, lime, cyan and violet. Use real food photography on dark cards, Geist for UI and a serif for the product name on the end card.

Banned: crossfades, blur-ins, 3D, particles, camera moves that reverse direction, holds longer than 1s, anything that feels like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
130 BPM, 32 beats (14.8s). Start the song 12 beats before its drop.

Beats 0-6, ask: push slowly into the glowing composer, about 3x zoom. Type the request over three fixed lines with a natural keystroke rhythm:
"I'm really hungry, I don't know
what I want but something
spicy, crispy and filling"

Beat 6, send: press the send button. A lime ripple spreads from it and transforms the message into a chat bubble. Pull back once to reveal the phone around it (428x900 screen, 11px black bezel, 9:41 status bar).

Beats 6-12, think: the send button grows into an orange wok, a half-disc with a thin handle. It tosses 6 colorful ingredients on beats 8, 9, 10 and 11 beneath the shimmering text "Finding something for you…".

Beat 12, the drop: a lime circle expands from the wok to fill the frame in about 0.35s. Dark food cards (330x440, radius 28, photo on top, name, one-line description, price and rating) burst in from the center. Slide the strip across three cards and land on "Fire Noodles", which lifts with a "Best match" pill.

Beats 16-21, chat: the lime contracts back into the user's bubble, carrying its words as the chosen card flies into its slot. "Found it. Fire Noodles from Wok & Fire, smoky, spicy and seriously filling." rises in, followed by "Want me to order it for you?" Then show two pills: "Order now" in black and "More options" outlined. The cursor clicks Order now → spinner → "✓ Ordered".

Beats 21-32, outro: the black button expands into the page, staying pill-shaped as it reaches the edges while the camera pushes into it. Its label grows to headline size, then slides away. Bring in "You were craving noodles." and "Now it's on the way." word by word (92px, white on black). A courier dot follows a route to a pin. The pin becomes the brand mark, and the wordmark wipes out from behind it, with "made with" above and the product name below.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, 1920x1080. Compute every style from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use one camera transform on a container, keyed by [time, zoom, x, y] with eased segments and zoom interpolated in log space.
3. Use closed-form step-response springs for every pop and settle.
4. Make every handoff a shared element: the lime flood carries a copy of the bubble's words, and the button carries its label into the page.
5. Sound: use a downloaded Mixkit SFX for each event - typing, send pop, each toss, drop impact, card swoosh, click, success tone, page-fill whoosh and mark sparkle. Place each by its measured peak and loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps using 8 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix. Review every fast moment frame by frame and scan the full video frame by frame.
</build>
entries.translated_prompt:
<输入项>
请向我询问：我的产品、用户在其中输入的确切请求、用于结果卡片的6到8张照片、一首约130 BPM且具有清晰高潮的免版税歌曲（来自Mixkit，可免费商用），以及用于结尾卡片的品牌标志。如果我跳过任何内容，请使用默认设置：下方的点餐故事、来自Pexels的食物照片（火鸡面、Birria塔可、辣味炸鸡、水牛城鸡翅、 Smash汉堡、辣味拉面），以及Mixkit的“Cat Walk”。
</输入项>

<指导>
一段15秒的产品发布影片，分辨率1920x1080，帧率60fps。仅限2D，单次连续拍摄。无淡入淡出、模糊或剪辑：每个场景都从上一个场景中生长出来。文字从遮罩线升起，按钮扩展成页面，颜色从一个物体涌入并在收缩成另一个物体前扩散。给相机每个场景一个缓动移动，并且不要连续进行放大和缩小。

外观：暖白色画布 (#f5f5f2)，黑色UI (#0e0e10)，石灰绿强调色 (#cdf24f)，橙色 (#ff6a2a)，以及蓝色发送按钮 (#2f6bff)。在输入框周围添加类似Apple Intelligence风格的虹彩光晕：一个模糊的圆锥渐变，旋转穿过粉色、橙色、石灰绿、青色和紫色。在深色卡片上使用真实的食物摄影，UI使用Geist字体，结尾卡片上的产品名称使用衬线字体。

禁止事项：交叉淡化、模糊进入、3D、粒子效果、方向反转的相机移动、超过1秒的停顿，以及任何感觉像模板的内容。
</指导>

<结构>
130 BPM，32拍（14.8秒）。在高潮前12拍开始播放音乐。

第0-6拍，提问：缓慢推近发光的输入框，大约3倍缩放。以自然的按键节奏在三行固定文本中输入请求：
“我真的饿了，我不知道
我想要什么，但想要一些
辛辣、酥脆且管饱的东西”

第6拍，发送：按下发送按钮。一道石灰绿的涟漪从中扩散，并将消息转化为聊天气泡。拉远一次以展示周围的手机（428x900屏幕，11px黑色边框，9:41状态栏）。

第6-12拍，思考：发送按钮长成一个橙色的炒锅，一个带有细手柄的半圆盘。它在闪烁的文字“正在为你寻找……”下方，在第8、9、10和11拍抛出6种彩色食材。

第12拍，高潮：一个石灰绿色的圆圈从炒锅扩大，在约0.35秒内填满画面。深色食物卡片（330x440，圆角半径28，顶部为照片，名称，一行描述，价格和评分）从中心爆发出现。滑动条带穿过三张卡片并停留在“火鸡面”上，它随着一个“最佳匹配”标签一起抬起。

第16-21拍，聊天：石灰绿色收缩回用户的消息气泡中，携带其文字，同时选中的卡片飞入其槽位。“找到了。来自Wok & Fire的火鸡面，烟熏、辛辣且非常管饱。”升起，随后是“要我帮你下单吗？”然后显示两个药丸状按钮：“立即下单”为黑色，“更多选项”为轮廓样式。光标点击立即下单 → 加载动画 → “✓ 已下单”。

第21-32拍，结尾：黑色按钮扩展成页面，保持药丸形状直到触及边缘，同时相机推进其中。其标签增长至标题大小，然后滑走。逐字引入“你当时想吃面条。”和“现在它已在路上。”（92px，黑底白字）。一个快递员点沿着路线跟随到一个图钉。图钉变成品牌标志，文字标识从其后方擦除消失，上方写着“由...制作”，下方写着产品名称。
</结构>

<构建>
1. 一个HTML文件，1920x1080。在seek(t)内部根据时间计算所有样式：不使用CSS过渡、计时器或帧间状态。
2. 在容器上使用单个相机变换，键值为[time, zoom, x, y]，具有缓动段，且缩放在对数空间中插值。
3. 对所有的弹出和静止使用闭式阶跃响应弹簧。
4. 使每一次交接成为一个共享元素：石灰绿洪水携带气泡文字的副本，按钮将其标签带入页面。
5. 声音：为每个事件使用下载的Mixkit音效 - 打字声、发送爆破声、每次抛掷声、高潮冲击声、卡片呼啸声、点击声、成功音调、页面填充呼啸声和标志闪光声。根据其测量峰值放置每一个，并将响度标准化为-14 LUFS。
6. 使用Playwright以60fps渲染，每帧使用8个子帧，并通过ffmpeg tmix混合。逐帧审查每个快速时刻并扫描完整视频的每一帧。
</构建>

entries.title: Pixel Art Voiceover Film Prompt
entries.description: A complex prompt for creating a 20-second 4:3 film with pixel art objects, heat-map silhouettes, and synchronized captions using Opus 5.5, including detailed direction and structure.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a voiceover or song with a spoken line (the audio file) and its transcript, 10-12 small objects that sum up my life, two silhouettes to light like a heat camera (a head in profile and a raised hand), and the 3 words I want to land hardest. If I skip any, use the defaults: vinyl, book, camera, cat, coin, game controller, cap, heart, money, plant, clapperboard, skateboard; free CC0 silhouettes from Openverse; action, intention, curiosity.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 20 second 4:3 film, 1440x1080 at 60fps, cut to the voice. Off-white paper, black, one red, one yellow, Geist for every word. Film grain on everything, a soft vignette, and a camera that never rests: a slow handheld float under everything plus a slow push inside every scene.
No scene cuts to the next: each handoff starts on the exact last frame of the scene before. The only hard cuts are the beat flips on the last word.
Every object is pixel art you draw yourself: a 16x16 grid per object, every cell a hand-placed colour, rendered as a 3D block (a darker extrusion down-right, a thin bevel on every cell) with a soft contact shadow.
The silhouettes are lit like a heat camera: the heat comes from how thick the body is at each point, so the nose, the hair and the fingertips run cooler, plus one hotspot and a slow moving noise, mapped through a black > red > orange > cream ramp. The edge stays razor sharp, with a soft glow outside it.
Motion rules: nothing pops in (eased glides of about 0.5s with a soft start), fast moves get real motion blur instead of ghost copies, and captions type with the voice behind a block cursor.
Banned: stock footage, AI video, 3D camera moves, particles, glitch.
</direction>

<structure>
Hang every scene on the transcript's word timings (measure them with faster-whisper word timestamps, one short chunk at a time):
1. The first word fills a yellow card. The card wipes off to the left and the question types underneath on two centred lines that glide to stay centred as they grow, the key word underlined in red as it's spoken.
2. The objects streak past in lanes above and below the words, a cyan four-point flare sweeps in, then the page burns away: black closes in from the edges onto the head, behind a hot red edge.
3. The head heats up on black while the answer types low on the left. A thin white orbit draws itself around the head, its far half passing behind it. On the last word, paper blooms out from inside the head with the objects in it, and the camera falls through: the head rushes past the lens until the paper is all we see.
4. The objects sit on a tilted ring seen in perspective (the front ones bigger and lower, drawn last), slowly turning, each one bobbing; the coin flips and lands with sparks.
5. On each of the 3 words, that object flies out of the ring to the left and grows, the page floods black from it, and the word types beside it (camera: a red shutter star; book: a red ribbon sweep; record: two white orbits and red notes). Then the flood drains back into the object as it flies home, and the camera dives closer into the ring. Put each hero object in the slot that is front-left when its word lands.
6. The ring pulls in a touch, bursts outward, every object turns to ink, and ink blots grow and swallow the page.
7. The hand rises into frame, hot, with the line split either side of it. The heart drops into its palm, then lifts to the centre at the size the next scene holds it.
8. The last word, one letter per beat, the background flipping paper / black / red, the heart holding its place across the cut, the centre object morphing pixel by pixel into the next one.
9. Thin brush strokes sweep through, the letters drift apart and float, then settle back into the word with the heart above it. The camera keeps pushing through the hold.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. Bake each pixel sprite once to an offscreen canvas (the extrusion layers, then the face), then draw it scaled and rotated.
3. The heat: precompute each silhouette's base heat once (a distance transform of the mask, held at the edge value outside it so nothing dark bleeds in when it is upscaled). Every frame, add the hotspot and two octaves of value noise at quarter resolution, map it through a 256-step lookup, upscale it, and cut it with the full-resolution mask.
4. The fall through the head: draw the ring scene into an offscreen layer, mask it with the head scaled up about a point inside the skull, and grow that scale on a cubed curve until the head covers the frame. The ring inside zooms less than the head does, so it reads as depth.
5. The pixel morph: pair every cell of object A with a cell of object B and glide each one's position and colour, with a small random delay per cell.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes, then lay the original audio back on with ffmpeg.
</build>

<gotchas>
A mask PNG with no alpha channel fills the whole box with heat, so put the silhouette in the alpha. A limb cut by the photo's border shows as a straight edge, so extend the mask past the frame. A handoff only reads as smooth when the last frame of one scene is the first frame of the next: draw the outgoing scene under the transition, and give scenes that show the same ring one shared zoom function. A flood that's still retreating when the next scene starts reads as a hard cut, so let it finish first. A fast ease-out flood reads as a jump; use a soft start.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, measure the word timings, then show me 8 stills before you render.
</start>

entries.title: Self-Building 3D House Animation
entries.description: Description of an interactive 3D house construction simulation built with One HTML file, Three.js, and WebGPU. Features timeline scrubbing, X-ray mode, explode view, and cutaway tools.
entries.prompt:
No plugins, no app, just a single HTML file running Three.js on WebGPU.

It's an interactive 3D house that builds itself in five stages: Foundation → Skeleton → Systems → Envelope → Finished. Every part has its own window on the timeline, so you can scrub through the construction like a video.

What's inside:
→ X-ray mode that makes the structure transparent and shows the water, power, sewage and airflow routes, with filters for each system
→ Explode, to pull the layers apart
→ Cut, a section plane that slices through the building
→ Dusk, a lighting switch to see it at night
→ Instanced vegetation, so a dozen olive trees cost almost nothing to render
→ Callouts and preset cameras for each stage

The subject is a traditional hillside villa, but the format works for any building. A developer could show a buyer exactly what's behind the walls before a single wall exists.

entries.description: A comprehensive set of 15 reusable prompts for generating various styles of code-rendered videos (shadow puppets, isometric flows, whiteboard animations, etc.) using Claude Opus 5.5.
entries.prompt:
做一支 10 秒彩色皮影戏，讲【曹冲称象】。剪影布局，暖光透背，关节式偶戏。依次出现秤盘、铜碗、石头，先平衡，再把石头分批称、加起来。字幕卡点出现。用代码渲染，导出可播放视频。

做一支 12 秒等距 2.5D 流程动画，讲【快递怎么分拣】。包裹沿分拣线、货台、平板运输、清关关卡移动，每步编号标签，最后双线汇成一条。干净、可跟读。

做一支 10 秒比例尺对比，把【地球、木星、太阳】按真实半径同屏摆放。镜头平滑拉远，第一个物体缩小，点题「太阳底下约有 130 万个地球」。数字标注清晰。

做一支 10 秒白板手绘。白底黑马克笔一笔笔画出【火柴人连甩 5 个包子】，红色只强调关键点。满足感粒子一颗比一颗大，最后角落画满。字幕：第 1 个，满足感拉满。

做一支 10 秒 WebGL 电影感汉字演变，主题【火】。龟甲、青铜、墨迹、火光质感。「火」从甲骨到闪电、火把，再到现代照明，形态连续变形，对应炎、烈、焰。

用 three.js 做一支 12 秒爆炸图，拆解【一部手机】。外壳、中框、芯片分层炸开，镜头环绕拉近，零件用虚线引出标注。可换成任何结构。

做一支 10 秒 16 位像素典故，讲【黄粱一梦】。取象、中举、治河、出征，每段约 1.6 秒硬切，最后回到现实。字幕：第二年，考中进士，当上了官。

做一支 10 秒绘本风科普，讲【小金鱼怎么游】。蜡笔线加铅笔涂色，线条抖动，眼睛、鳃、尾鳍对称，尾巴跟着节拍摆。纸本质感。

做一支 10 秒 3Blue1Brown 式数学可视化，讲【圆面积】。深色底，圆切成 8、16、32 个扇形，真的移拼成长方形。公式逐项出现，定格 πr²。

做一支 10 秒古地图动画，讲【长安到敦煌】。羊皮纸、淡墨山路，朱红路线一笔画过去，标注里程和一句讲解，最后盖章。镜头可缩放。

做一支 10 秒 Kurzgesagt 式信息图，讲【纸对折厚度】。干净图形、大数字：对折 2 次，厚度 0.4 毫米，厚度 ×2。镜头规则拉近，直到终点。

做一支 10 秒扁平 MG，讲【降水】。纯色几何、无描边。云里的小水滴越聚越大，然后掉下来。两段明暗，卡通云朵。

做一支 10 秒卡点排版，120 BPM，讲【费曼学习法】。每个词卡一拍，黑底橙字切入。四步依次砸出，最后一锤：讲不清楚，就是没真懂。

做一支 10 秒漫画分格，讲【一扇窗破了】。黑白网点加一个红色。听课、被发现、冲出教室，格间硬切，最后一格点题。

做一支 12 秒横轴时间线，讲【从达特茅斯到 ChatGPT】。镜头沿轴推进，节点缩放点亮。年份大字加一句事件。示例节点：1971，又过了 41 年。

entries.title: Tile Assembly Ad Video Prompt
entries.description: A detailed Japanese prompt for creating a 30-second tile assembly advertisement video using Claude Opus 5.5, Three.js, and ffmpeg.
entries.prompt:
添付の画像を「最後の画面」にして、全部タイルでできた30秒の広告動画（音つき・mp4）を作ってください。
ブラウザ（Three.js）で組み、Chromeで全コマを書き出し、ffmpegでmp4にします。

# ゴール
- 見る人は25秒、タイルの制作動画だと思って見る。最後の数秒で、添付画像（広告）だったと気づく
- 最後の画面は添付画像とほぼ同じ。文字が読める。画面いっぱいがタイル（床は見せない）

# 仕様
- 1920×1080、30fps、30秒。HTML1ファイル（Three.js。npmで入れてesbuildで1ファイルに固める）
- 時刻 t を渡すと、同じ t なら必ず同じ絵になる作りにする（seek(t)）
- タイルは1枚ずつ別のインスタンス。16:9の格子で約19万枚（576×324）
- 位置・向き・厚み・面取り・色を1枚ずつ変える。目地（隙間）は空き。線は引かない
- 添付画像は、タイルの色を取るためだけに使う（テクスチャとして貼らない）
- 素材は約12種（釉薬セラミック、スレート、真珠貝、白磁、テラコッタ、ガラスなど）。色の明るさと彩度で割り当てる
- 光は、左上の硬い太陽1つ。床は漆喰。奥に赤い大工のチョーク線がピンぼけで入る
- 被写界深度（円形ボケ）を後処理で自作する。しぼりは最初大きく、最後は小さく

# 流れ（秒）
0〜3　 床に暗いタイルが1枚。カメラは床すれすれ
3〜10　[組み始める場所]から、タイルが渦を巻いて落ちる。最初の1枚→周りの順に増える
10〜21 一気に外へ広がる。カメラが引いて[見せたい絵]が見えてくる
21〜24 全体が見える。文字になる場所は、周りと同じ淡い色のまま
24〜26 文字・ロゴ・ボタンのタイルが、左から順にパタパタ裏返って現れる
26〜30 真上からの構図で止まる。カーソルが[ボタンの文言]をクリックし、ボタンのタイルが少し沈む

# ハマりどころ（必ず守る）
- 文字になるタイルは、最初は周りの背景色で組む。背景色は、外側から内側へ塗り広げて決める。文字のふち（白ぶち）も一緒に裏返す。守らないと、途中で文字の形が見えてしまう
- 真上のカメラは、位置を真上ぴったりにしない（向きが90°回る）。止める所は、動きの勢いをゼロにする（補間のはみ出しで反転する）
- 最後の画面は、元画像と並べて色を比べ、露出・彩度・色味を合わせる
- 文字が小さくて読めないときは、タイル数を増やす
- 下地の暗い面は、タイルが着地したマスだけに出す

# 音
- ElevenLabsの効果音で、タイルを置く音・裏返す音・マウスのクリックを作る（各0.5秒）。作る前に、クレジットの消費を知らせる
- タイルの着地・裏返しの時刻に合わせて並べて重ねる。カメラが遠いほど小さく、数が増えたら雨のようにまとめる
- 24〜26秒のパタパタを、いちばん目立たせる。音量は -16 LUFS

# 進め方
1. 先に脚本（秒ごとの情景）を日本語で出し、OKをもらってから作る
2. 途中のコマ（最初のタイル／組み始め／引き／全景／文字が出る瞬間／最後）を自分で見て直す
3. 書き出しは Chrome（puppeteer-core）で seek(t) を30fpsぶん呼び、png を ffmpeg に流す
4. 納品は mp4（高画質と共有用）と、確認した画像

# 入力
- エンドフレーム: [添付]
- 組み始める場所: [例：人物の目]
- 引いたときに見せたい絵: [例：笑顔の女性]
- ボタンの文言: [例：無料体験はこちら]
entries.translated_prompt:
Please create a 30-second advertisement video (with sound, MP4) made entirely of tiles, using the attached image as the "final screen".
Assemble it in a browser (Three.js), export all frames via Chrome, and convert to MP4 using ffmpeg.

# Goal
- Viewers watch for 25 seconds thinking it's a tile production video. In the last few seconds, they realize it was the attached image (advertisement).
- The final screen is almost identical to the attached image. Text is readable. The entire screen is filled with tiles (do not show the floor).

# Specifications
- 1920x1080, 30fps, 30 seconds. Single HTML file (Three.js. Install via npm and bundle into one file with esbuild).
- Design so that passing time t always results in the same image for the same t (seek(t)).
- Tiles are separate instances. Approximately 190,000 tiles in a 16:9 grid (576x324).
- Change position, orientation, thickness, chamfering, and color for each tile individually. Leave gaps (mortar). Do not draw lines.
- Use the attached image only to extract colors for the tiles (do not apply as texture).
- About 12 materials (glazed ceramic, slate, pearl shell, white porcelain, terracotta, glass, etc.). Assign based on color brightness and saturation.
- Lighting: One hard sun from the top left. Floor is plaster. Red carpenter chalk lines appear blurred in the background.
- Create depth of field (circular bokeh) via post-processing. Aperture starts large and ends small.

# Flow (Seconds)
0-3: One dark tile on the floor. Camera skims the floor.
3-10: Tiles spiral down starting from [Start Assembly Location]. Increase from the first tile outward.
10-21: Spread rapidly outward. Camera pulls back to reveal [Desired Image].
21-24: Full view visible. Areas that will become text remain pale like the surroundings.
24-26: Tiles for text, logo, and buttons flip over from left to right.
26-30: Stop with a top-down composition. Cursor clicks [Button Text], and button tiles sink slightly.

# Pitfalls (Must Follow)
- Tiles that will become text should initially be assembled with surrounding background colors. Determine background colors by spreading from outside to inside. Flip the text borders (white edges) together. If not followed, text shapes might be visible midway.
- Do not place the top camera exactly overhead (orientation rotates 90 degrees). When stopping, zero out motion momentum (prevent inversion due to interpolation overshoot).
- Compare the final screen side-by-side with the original image to match exposure, saturation, and color tone.
- If text is too small to read, increase the number of tiles.
- Show dark base surfaces only on squares where tiles have landed.

# Sound
- Create sounds for placing tiles, flipping them, and mouse clicks using ElevenLabs effects (0.5s each). Notify credit consumption before creation.
- Layer sounds aligned with tile landing and flipping times. Make them quieter as the camera gets farther; group many sounds like rain if numerous.
- Emphasize the flipping sound at 24-26 seconds. Volume at -16 LUFS.

# Process
1. First provide a script (scene per second) in Japanese, get approval, then build.
2. Review and fix intermediate frames (first tile/start/pull-back/full view/text appearance/final) yourself.
3. Export using Chrome (puppeteer-core) calling seek(t) for 30fps worth, piping pngs to ffmpeg.
4. Deliver MP4 (high quality and shared version) and verified images.

# Inputs
- End Frame: [Attached]
- Start Assembly Location: [Example: Person's eye]
- Desired Image when Pulled Back: [Example: Smiling woman]
- Button Text: [Example: Try Free Here]

entries.title: Interactive 3D Mechanical Watch Animation
entries.description: Generates a realistic interactive 3D mechanical watch using Three.js in a single HTML file. Includes complex animations like the swinging balance wheel, ticking gears, and an explode view with labeled parts.
entries.prompt:
Build me a mechanical watch in interactive 3D, in one HTML file with Three.js.

Make it look real: the gold case and the glass on top, the dial and the hands, and behind it the movement you never get to see. The mainspring in its barrel, the gear train, the balance wheel swinging back and forth with its hairspring breathing, the escape wheel and the pallet fork ticking, and the red jewels the gears turn on. The balance wheel swings, the gears turn, and the second hand ticks. I can drag to orbit around it and scroll to zoom.

Add an Explode button. When I press it, every part slides apart in layers with its name on a label. Press it again and it all snaps back together. When I hover a part, it lights up and shows one line on what it does.

No images. Do not ask me any questions. Just build it.

entries.title: Product Promo Motion Video Prompt
entries.description: A prompt template for Claude Opus 5.5 to create a 22-second product promo video with complex morphing animations and beat-synced transitions in HTML.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: one question a user asks my product and its one-line answer, two album covers, a royalty-free song around 110 BPM with a quiet intro and a hard drop (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and my logo for the ending. If I skip anything, use these defaults: "is this all code?" / "yes. every frame.", two atmospheric photos, and Mixkit "Head Bang".
</inputs>

<direction>
A 22-second square loop, 1440x1440 at 60fps. 2D only, one continuous take. Nothing cuts: each scene grows from the one before it, and every gesture carries the camera into the next space. Each morph takes 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1). The camera zoom follows the same curve, making the shape changes feel almost invisible. Content dissolves during the second half of each glide. One gesture per scene.

Look: a warm light stage (#f3f3f0 to #e3e3de), black UI, and a dark app world (#121212) tinted by the current album cover. Use one green accent (#1ed760), Geist for UI, the real macOS pointer, and soft layered shadows that grow as shapes lift.

Banned: hard cuts, bouncy springs, particles, glows, zooming in and immediately back out, holds longer than 1s, anything that feels like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
Follow the song's beats. The press lands on the drop.

Generate: the cursor clicks. The pill glides into a spinner, then becomes a check.

Chat: the check splits into three typing dots with goo. The left dot flies up, becomes the question bubble and types the question. The right dot flies down into the reply. Both bubbles shrink back into dots as they glide toward the center and merge with the middle dot.

Play: the middle dot bends into a play triangle, one point at a time. The cursor presses it on the drop. A white button appears under the click as the dark app floods the frame around it, leaving the white shape as the play button. The camera pulls back to reveal the full now-playing screen: large cover, title, heart (liked, filling green), progress bar, controls and volume.

Swipe: the cursor drags the cover sideways. The next track slides in, and the app changes its tint to match the new cover.

Drag: the camera glides toward the volume slider. The cursor pulls it to max and keeps going. The bar rubber-bands, dragging the camera sideways out of the app and onto a dark dotted canvas while the camera follows the knob.

Chart: the line lands and curves upward into a green chart as the number counts up. The volume knob becomes the chart's final point.

Dive: the cursor clicks that point. The camera dives into it until the light stage fills the frame.

Ending: an "Ask [my product]" button grows from the light, narrows into a line, then fans out into my logo (default: the Claude spark, with six copies rotating into twelve rays in Claude orange). Hold for 2s.

entries.title: Product Launch Film Prompt Template
entries.description: A comprehensive prompt template for generating a continuous product launch UI motion film in a single HTML file, detailing scene transitions, timing, and rendering instructions.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a one-word product name for the wordmark, one accent color, and a royalty-free track around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Product-launch UI motion in one continuous take. One shape tells the whole story: a prompt bar becomes a button, the button becomes a progress ring, the ring becomes a preview window, the window fills the screen, then shrinks into a toast and back into the prompt bar. No cuts, no fades between scenes: objects transform. A cursor triggers every change with real clicks. Warm off-white canvas, black UI, one accent color, Inter for UI and the wordmark. Springs everywhere with only a slight overshoot. Zoom the camera so each moment fills the square.
Banned: crossfades, gradients on UI, particles, glows, bouncy easing, dead beats, anything that feels like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 24 beats, something happens on every beat.
Type the request into the prompt bar → click send → the bar collapses into a black circle → a progress ring fills in four steps while four chips spring out (concept, storyboard, motion, sound) → the chips fly into a timeline and the circle becomes a preview window → a playhead sweeps the clips → inside the preview an orbit draws itself, a planet starts moving and the wordmark rises letter by letter from a mask line → the preview fills the screen → the letters drop away, the planet flies into a toast and becomes its checkmark → "Rendered in code · 60 fps" → the toast turns back into an empty prompt bar. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file with a 1440x1440 canvas. Draw everything inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use closed-form spring step responses. When a value changes target several times, add one spring per change so it stays a pure function of time.
3. The main shape is one rounded rect whose width, height, radius, position and color are each a chain of springs.
4. Typing is derived from time: characters shown = floor(progress × length), with a caret that blinks only when idle.
5. Find the beat grid of the track, start on a downbeat and place every click, pop and chime on its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright at 60 fps, then encode H.264 CRF 16 and loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render one still per beat first. Fix anything cramped, off-grid or hard to read before the full render.
</build>

<gotchas>
Text inside a morphing shape needs its own clip and separate enter/exit timing. Text swaps need their own fade so they never overlap. The cursor must end at the exact position it started, or the loop will stutter.
</gotchas>

entries.title: Motion Design System Prompt
entries.description: A prompt for Claude Opus 5.5 to create a 15-second motion design film demonstrating a system starting from an orange dot, covering typography, springs, shapes, and kinetic type.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a short label for the opening toggle, one hero word, a percentage for the graph, the text for the final card, one accent color, and a track with a clear beat.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 2D motion design film in 16:9. Use a warm off-white canvas, near-black backgrounds, bold typography and one vivid orange accent. The orange dot connects every scene: it starts in the UI, becomes the dot over a letter, traces a spring graph, grows into a shape and returns on the end card. A cursor makes the opening click feel real. Keep the motion sharp and controlled, with small spring overshoots and no dead time.
Banned: stock footage, gradients, glows, particle bursts, random transitions and motion that isn't connected to an element already on screen.
</direction>

<structure>
Around 15 seconds, with a visual change on every major beat.
Open: a cursor clicks the orange toggle beside "Reduce Motion". The letters bend and move into place until only "Motion" remains, with the orange dot above the "i".
Spring: the dot jumps away from the word and lands on a graph. Its path draws a spring response, overshoots the target and settles beside a "+22%" callout.
Shape: the dot shoots across a line, grows into an orange circle and fills the frame. A black rounded square rotates inside it, then stretches into a pill. The scene contracts to a single orange dot on black.
Type: words like "SPRINGS", "EASING", "KINETIC TYPE", "3D" and "SOUND" orbit the dot. The circle of type opens out into a field of tiny dots.
Reveal: the halftone field expands and flips to black, revealing the final card: "Opus 5.5", "Motion designer." and "0 keyframes".
Return: the orange dot moves back through the halftone, graph and toggle. Match the final frame to the first so the video loops cleanly.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, 1920x1080 at 60fps. Compute every visual from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use closed-form springs for the toggle, bouncing dot and graph. Draw the graph from the same spring function that moves the dot.
3. Animate letters individually for the "Reduce Motion" to "Motion" transformation. Keep the orange dot attached to the "i" until it begins its jump.
4. Make the orange circle, rotating square and pill different states of the same shape. Preserve its position and motion through each transformation.
5. Place the orbiting words along a circular path, then move their letters outward to hand the frame over to the halftone grid.
6. Draw the halftone as a grid of dots whose sizes respond to the orange dot. Let it grow past the frame edges before revealing the end card.
7. Sync the click, dot landing, graph peak, shape changes and final title to measured beats.

entries.title: Particle Effect Video Workflow
entries.description: A comprehensive workflow guide for creating particle effect videos using Opus 5.5, covering material selection, frame extraction, particle styling, rhythm detection, and timeline arrangement.
entries.prompt:
公开我的制作方案，发给Opus5.5就能用

  1. 选素材

  三个标准，直接决定成败：

  - 主体完整：人物或物体全身入画。细节会在加工中丢失，观众靠轮廓认东西，特写会变成一团。
  - 背景干净：纯色、雪地、天空都行，主体和背景容易分开。
  - 有明确的动作瞬间：打击、起跳、落地、转身。这些是后面做特效的支点。

  来源可以是自己拍的、视频模型生成的，或有授权的现成片段。

  2. 拆素材

  从每一帧提取三类信息：

  - 颜色：原画面。
  - 远近：每个位置离镜头多远，用现成的深度估计模型算。
  - 主体范围：哪里是主体、哪里是背景。

  另外找出镜头切换发生在哪些时刻。这一步的要点是保持稳定：远近和主体范围要在同一个镜头内统一处理，否则播放起来会抖。

  3. 定"粒子"和"样式"

  先决定用什么东西来重建画面：圆点、方块、文字、线条都可以。

  然后设计几种样式。每种样式其实只是三条规则的不同组合：

  - 放在哪：整个画面都放，还是只放在主体上。
  - 多大：统一大小，还是跟着明暗、远近变化。
  - 什么颜色：用原画的颜色，还是统一用一两种颜色。

  再加一个开关：是平铺在一个面上，还是按远近推进三维空间。推进去之后镜头才能环绕。

  准备四到六种差异明显的样式就够用。粒子的疏密需要自己看着调：太大认不出内容，太小又和原片没区别。

  4. 找节奏

  - 定速度：选定音乐的速度，把时间切成等长的小格。让一格正好是整数帧，后面所有切换都好对齐。
  - 找动作瞬间：结合"声音突然变响"和"画面突然变动"两个信号，找出素材里的打击点。
  - 准备音乐：可以用现成的曲子并分析出它的拍子，也可以按定好的速度合成一段，并在打击点上加重音。

  5. 编排

  做一张时间表，写明每一格用哪种样式、什么配色、镜头在哪。这张表单独存放，以后调节奏只改它。

  编排的四条原则：

  - 开头交代变化：先给原画面，再过渡到粒子，让观众看懂发生了什么。
  - 快慢交替：一直快会麻木，中间要有一段明显慢下来的部分。
  - 配色要撞：相邻两格的颜色和样式反差越大，切换越有力。
  - 结尾要有收束：比如粒子越来越大直到变成色块，或者回到原画面。

  6. 关键时刻的反馈

  在打击点上叠加短促的反应，按轻重分级：

  - 每一次都有的轻反馈：粒子变形一下、镜头顶一下。
  - 较重时才有的中反馈：一部分粒子朝镜头弹开。
  - 最重的一两次才用的大反馈：时间静止，镜头环绕。

  原则是弱而短。只动一部分粒子，几帧内结束，否则画面炸成一片，观众就看不清主体在做什么了。

  贯穿全程的工作方法

  - 先小样后全片：每做完一个环节，先渲染几帧看效果，确认了再往下。全片只在最后渲染。
  - 拿不准的参数一次出一排：比如疏密，让 AI 同时出五六个档位并排放，你来挑。
  - 改哪里渲哪里：调整某一段时只重新渲染那一段。
  - 让 AI 自己看图：每一步都要求它把渲染结果打开看一遍再汇报。
  - 所有随机都固定：保证同样的设置每次渲染结果一致，否则没法逐步修改。
entries.translated_prompt:
Share my production plan, send it to Opus 5.5 and it works.

1. Select Materials
Three standards determine success:
- Complete Subject: Full body of person or object in frame. Details are lost during processing; viewers recognize things by outline, close-ups become blurry.
- Clean Background: Solid color, snow, sky, etc., making subject/background separation easy.
- Clear Action Moments: Strikes, jumps, landings, turns. These are anchor points for special effects.
Sources can be self-shot, video model generated, or licensed clips.

2. Deconstruct Materials
Extract three types of info from each frame:
- Color: Original image.
- Depth: Distance from camera per position, calculated using depth estimation models.
- Subject Range: Where is the subject vs background.
Also identify shot transition moments. Key is stability: depth and subject range must be processed uniformly within the same shot to avoid jitter.

3. Define "Particles" and "Styles"
Decide what rebuilds the image: dots, squares, text, lines.
Design several styles. Each style is a combination of three rules:
- Placement: Entire image or only on subject.
- Size: Uniform or varying with brightness/depth.
- Color: Original colors or unified one/two colors.
Add a switch: Flat plane or 3D space based on depth. 3D allows camera orbiting.
Prepare 4-6 distinct styles. Adjust particle density visually: too large obscures content, too small looks like original.

4. Find Rhythm
- Set Speed: Choose music tempo, cut time into equal grids. Ensure one grid equals integer frames for alignment.
- Find Action Moments: Combine audio spikes and visual changes to find beats/strikes.
- Prepare Music: Analyze existing tracks or synthesize new ones matching speed, emphasizing beats.

5. Arrangement
Create a timeline specifying style, color scheme, and camera position for each grid. Store separately for easy rhythm adjustments.
Four principles:
- Intro Transition: Show original first, then transition to particles so viewers understand the change.
- Fast/Slow Alternation: Avoid monotony; include clearly slower sections.
- Contrast Colors: High contrast between adjacent grids makes transitions powerful.
- Ending Convergence: Particles grow into blocks or return to original image.

6. Feedback at Key Moments
Overlay short reactions on beats, graded by intensity:
- Light (every beat): Particle deformation, slight camera push.
- Medium (heavier beats): Some particles bounce toward camera.
- Heavy (climax): Time freeze, camera orbit.
Principle: Weak and short. Move only some particles, end within few frames, otherwise screen explodes and subject is unclear.

Work Method Throughout
- Small Sample First: Render few frames after each step to verify before proceeding. Full render only at end.
- Batch Parameters: For uncertain params like density, have AI generate 5-6 levels side-by-side for you to choose.
- Partial Re-render: Only re-render adjusted segments.
- Visual Check: Require AI to open and view rendered results before reporting.
- Fix Randomness: Ensure consistent rendering for identical settings to allow iterative modification.

entries.title: Euclid's Proof Kinetic Typography
entries.description: A prompt for Claude Opus 5.5 to create a kinetic mathematical proof animation titled 'There Is No Last Prime', using mechanical inspection metaphors, SVG/Canvas, and specific typography rules.
entries.prompt:
Create a kinetic mathematical proof titled “THERE IS NO LAST PRIME.”
Stage Euclid’s argument as a beautiful mechanical inspection system. Typography becomes engraved number wheels, multiplication belts, and remainder indicators.
The mechanism must demonstrate the proof rather than decorate a narrated explanation.
DELIVERABLE
One self-contained HTML file.
1080×1080.
20.00-second loop.
Deterministic 60fps rendering.
Use SVG and/or Canvas.
No external runtime assets.
PALETTE
Porcelain # F0EEE6.
Graphite #222522.
Industrial green # 416B53.
Warning orange # E78636.
TYPE
Tabular monospace for all calculations.
Heavy geometric grotesque for declarations.
Small technical serif for the final logical statement.
Use disciplined spacing and large, readable numerals.
LOCKED COPY
SUPPOSE THE LIST ENDS.
MULTIPLY EVERY PRIME ON IT.
ADD ONE.
EVERY LISTED PRIME LEAVES REMAINDER 1.
A PRIME FACTOR IS MISSING.
THERE IS NO LAST PRIME.
CENTRAL EXAMPLE
Assumed list:
2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13
Product:
30030
Product plus one:
30031
Factorization:
30031 = 59 × 509
Both factors are absent from the assumed list.
IMPORTANT LOGIC
Do not claim that multiplying primes and adding one always produces a prime.
The constructed number may be composite.
Its prime factors cannot be any prime on the assumed complete list.
The numerical example illustrates the general contradiction.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.00
SUPPOSE THE LIST ENDS.
Six engraved prime wheels lock into a finite inspection rack.
A physical end-stop closes after 13.
The end-stop makes the claim of completeness visible.
3.00–6.50
MULTIPLY EVERY PRIME ON IT.
A belt couples all six wheels.
Show a readable multiplication expression:
2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 = 30030.
Use rolling numerals only during movement; settle the final value sharply.
6.50–8.50
ADD ONE.
A single orange unit enters the mechanism.
It advances the output from 30030 to 30031.
Make this one-unit change the decisive visual event.
8.50–12.50
EVERY LISTED PRIME LEAVES REMAINDER 1.
The output passes through six division gates.
Each gate is labelled with its prime.
Each produces the same visible remainder: 1.
Arrange the six completed results so the audience can compare them simultaneously.
12.50–15.50
The output opens as a labelled mechanical casing.
Inside, reveal:
59 × 509.
These factors cannot fit into the supposedly complete rack.
The end-stop is forced outward by the new factor cards.
15.50–18.00
A PRIME FACTOR IS MISSING.
Then:
THERE IS NO LAST PRIME.
Hold the general statement above the opened rack.
Include the compact general form:
N = p₁p₂…pₖ + 1.
N mod pᵢ = 1.
18.00–20.00
A fresh inspection plate slides over the mechanism.
Its engraved edge becomes the original end-stop.
Reset the hidden wheels.
Reveal the opening rack at the exact initial position.
REQUIRED MOTION
Every mechanical action must correspond to an operation in the proof.
Use linked rota

entries.description: A prompt for generating a 30-second hand-drawn style animation using pure code (SVG vector graphics and synthesized audio) with Claude Opus 5.5. entries.prompt:
Create a 30-second full-code-driven animation using SVG vector graphics and synthesized original soundtrack. 

Visual Style: Abandon line boiling; use hand-written vector gradients, soft shadows, and night sky glows.

Scene Sequence:
1. A small character steps on the ground, charges up, runs into the sunset, and hits a star which explodes.

entries.title: Code-Generated Music Video Animation Prompt
entries.description: A comprehensive prompt for Claude Opus 5.5 to create a complete music video using JavaScript animations, driven by an existing song and starter repository.
entries.prompt:
Make a complete music video for the song in this folder, with all
visuals drawn and animated in JavaScript. Use the entire song.

SETUP
Inspect this folder and identify the song and any lyrics or reference
files. Preserve my original files unchanged.

Use this existing animation starter:
https://t.co/oN3A7ZZyEl

Clone it into a new ./video subfolder, unless an existing copy is
already present. Do not overwrite existing work or clone into the
nonempty project root.

Read its README.md and ANIMATION_GUIDE.md completely, then inspect
render.mjs and the project configuration. Use the existing rendering
machinery rather than inventing a replacement.

Check Node.js, Chrome, and FFmpeg. Inspect the package configuration
and install the project dependencies. Ask before making system-wide
changes or downloading large additional tools.

Do not use fal, external image/video generation, paid APIs, or the
hybrid music-video plugin. All finished visuals must be code-drawn.

CREATIVE DIRECTION
Create a cohesive, visually imaginative animated music video with a
handmade, papery, illustrated feel. Express the song's meaning through
scenes, characters, visual metaphors, and purposeful transitions.
Establish an engaging opening and develop recurring visual motifs.
Do not make a slideshow, a generic audio visualizer, or one animation
loop repeated for the entire song. Design characters appropriate to
this song rather than automatically using the starter's mascot.

MUSIC AND TIMING
Use the supplied recording as the continuous master soundtrack.
Do not remix, replace, speed up, or shorten it.

Measure its duration and use available local audio-analysis tools to
identify musical sections and likely beat/accent timings. Record these
in a shared timeline and drive animation from that timeline.

Use supplied lyrics as authoritative. If lyrics are missing, use a
local transcription tool only if available, flag uncertain words, and
do not invent lyrics. Continue with non-lyric visuals where necessary.

When verified lyrics are available, use expressive, readable lyric
animation where it strengthens the scene. This explicitly overrides
the starter's default preference against lettering.

PRODUCTION
Write STORYBOARD.md with timed scenes covering the complete recording.
Save the project brief and rerender instructions in CLAUDE.md.

Then build the video. Make reasonable creative decisions and continue
without stopping for approval at every scene.

Test a few representative frames and a short section before the full
render. Inspect the resulting images and frame sequences, fix visible
defects, and keep the animation practical for this computer.

Use efficient code-drawn textures if expensive watercolor effects
make rendering impractical.

DELIVERY
Render the complete video

entries.title: Launch Trailer Video Generation Prompt
entries.description: A detailed prompt for creating a 25-second launch trailer video using Claude Opus 5.5, specifying inputs like product name, tagline, story steps, colors, fonts, motion rules, and scene structure.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product's name (one lowercase word), a 4-word tagline, the 3-step story of what it does, a launch date and domain, a royalty-free song with a clear drop, 4 vertical talking-to-camera clips and 12 portrait photos. If I skip any, use the defaults: "castr", "ugc ads, cast by ai", write a brief → scan 1,000 creators → cast 4, Mixkit "Cat Walk" (129.6 BPM, drop at 29.7s), free Pexels clips and portraits, and transparent stickers from Pixabay (serum, mic, megaphone, vintage camera, spotlight, lips).
</inputs>

<direction>
A 25 second square launch trailer, 1440x1440 at 60fps, loud poster style. Cobalt #2B3BFF, ink #0E0F1F, cream #F6E4C6, pink #FF7DC7, tangerine #FF5A1F. Archivo 900 extra-condensed for names, expanded for headlines, Geist and Geist Mono for labels. Op-art sunburst, scrolling waves, film grain. Real media only: the clips play inside the design, and the stickers get a white die-cut border and a soft shadow.
Motion rules: the camera never stops (a slow 1.03-1.07 push on every scene), nothing pops in (letters rise through a mask line one by one), nothing snaps to the beat (patterns rotate continuously), swaps are carousel glides of about 0.55s, colour changes fade over about 0.35s, stickers ease in and then keep a slow sway. No full stops after the wordmark or any headline.
Banned: beat-snapped rotations, pop-in slams, white flashes, crossfades between scenes, hard cuts, templates.
</direction>

<structure>
54 beats. The song starts 8 beats before its drop.
Beats 0-8: a cobalt sunburst turns around a breathing cream disc. The wordmark types in with a gliding caret and the tagline pill rises. The disc floods the frame into the drop.
Beat 8, the drop: the cream becomes the face of a 3D box and "ONE BRIEF" rises letter by letter. The camera pulls back to the box floating on waves. On beat 12 it turns to "1,000 CREATORS" (stacked, with outlined echoes), on beat 14 to "ZERO DMs".
Beats 16-22: a whip to a dark desk. A tangerine "BRIEF #042" ticket types its rows (product, vibe, cast, due), stickers drift on, a polaroid of a real clip drops onto the corner, and a "NOW CASTING" stamp presses down on beat 20.
Beats 22-34: the casting stage. A crowd of black and white portraits in an arc, a 3D stage block, and the creators gliding through like a carousel. Each plays live in a big disc in black and white, with their name in pink on the stage, their followers, and a MATCH % that counts up. One beat later a "CAST ✓" stamp lands and the clip fades to colour. A counter rolls 1/4 to 4/4.
Beats 34-39: pink floods out of the last disc. The disc morphs into a phone screen (the clip keeps playing) and fans into 4 phones playing all 4 creators, with views counting up. "4 ADS" and "BY FRIDAY" rise.
Beats 39-44, the music's break: the pink floor drops away and a cream "JOIN THE WAITLIST" ticket glides down onto the sunburst. On the pickup its stub tears off.
Beats 44-54: the ticket body morphs into a poster arch. The wordmark rises in, then the tagline, then an info bar slides up in 3 blocks (date, numbers, domain) and a ticker runs round the frame edge. Then it all folds back into the opening disc, so the last frame is the first.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. A beat map in beats, B = 60/BPM, with the song placed so its drop lands on beat 8.
3. The 3D box is an orthographic projection: each face is a 1440px offscreen canvas drawn with an affine transform and shaded by its normal.
4. Cut the clips to 30fps JPEG sequences with ffmpeg, draw frame floor(t*30), and do the black and white with ctx.filter.
5. Trim the sticker PNGs and add the die-cut border by dilating their alpha.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event (a shutter on every cast, whooshes on the glides, key clicks on the typing), each placed by its measured peak. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes. Scan for single-frame pops, then compare its motion against a reference video (hard jumps per second, share of still frames).
</build>

<gotchas>
A pattern that rotates one notch per beat reads as stutter: rotate it continuously, and pick each ring's speed so it lands on the same pattern at the last frame. 4 subframes ghost on fast whips, so use 8. A layer whose background is a huge flood circle still covers the screen after sliding down one frame height, so switch it to a full-frame rect once it has flooded. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's. The disc must morph inside the same camera transform as the scene it leaves, or it jumps.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 6 stills (open, box, brief, casting, phones, poster) before you render.
</start>

entries.title: Opus 5.5 Product Launch Motion Design Prompt
entries.description: A comprehensive prompt for creating a 24-second square product launch video using pure code (HTML Canvas) with Claude Opus 5.5. It details morph transitions, glassmorphism UI elements, precise timing based on music beats, and technical constraints like 60fps rendering and Playwright usage.
entries.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product's name ({argument name="product_name" default="nightshift"}) (one lowercase word, it becomes a black wordmark with a period), the one job a user hands it before bed ({argument name="user_job" default="book 10 sales calls this week"}), the three results it reports by morning ({argument name="results" default="200 leads found / 200 emails sent / 10 calls booked"}), two photos of the same place at night and by day (aligned, so a crossfade reads as a real sunrise), one sunny daytime photo for outside the logo, and a song with a big hit near its start. If I skip any, use the defaults.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 24 second square product launch video, 1440x1440 at 60fps, 2D only, one continuous take that loops. The whole video happens inside the period of the wordmark. Outside it's daytime (the sunny photo behind a black wordmark). Inside it's the night photo under iOS-style glass panels (the blurred photo behind each panel, a tint, a rim light). Nothing cuts: every scene grows out of the last, shapes morph, dots fly, colours change under floods. Every morph glides 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1) and the camera zoom rides the same curve. Geist, the real macOS pointer, soft shadows that grow with each shape's height.
Banned: flat or gradient backgrounds made in code, camera zooms into tiny points, hard cuts, crossfades between scenes, bouncy springs, particles, glows, holds longer than 1s, cropped type.
</direction>

<structure>
Beats are the song's. The song enters on its big hit as the first pill appears.
Open: the letters slide into the period and vanish into it while it glides to the middle. The period opens like an iris onto the night inside it, and "you log off at 6", then "{argument name="product_name_en" default="[product]"} doesn't", roll through one mask line over the night photo.
Ask: a glass "Ask {argument name="product_name_en" default="[product]"}" pill springs in. The cursor clicks it, it glides into an input and the job types out.
Find: send shrinks the input to a dot that ripples into a 23x15 grid. A scan line sweeps it, 200 dots light up and a counter counts them.
Write: the lit dots pour into a glass email composer. A second, purple cursor labelled "{argument name="product_name_en" default="[product]"}" types a personal opener and presses Send, and the counter runs to 200/200.
Night: the composer becomes a glass orb with a progress ring. A clock chip swaps 11:42 PM, 3:17 AM, 5:02 AM, 6:59 AM while the sky relights from night to dawn and "while you sleep" rolls in.
Results (beat 20): the orb turns black and goo-splits into the three result pills. The checks pop green.
Morning: the pills merge into a Dynamic Island that grows into a phone lock screen: the day photo, the date, a big 7:00, the bezel growing out of the screen edge. Three glass notifications stack in, and the cursor taps the first, which opens like iOS.
Proof: a week calendar (10 meetings pop in, a hover shows one's time), then a pipeline chart ($48,200 counts up, the line draws, a hover follows it). A black flood from the line's end becomes "Start your night shift →" and the cursor clicks it.
Out: the button shrinks into a dot, the whole scene closes down into it like an iris, and the letters slide back out of the period. The tagline rises. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Everything is a pure function of time inside seek(t): no timers, no state between frames.
2. One element morphs through every state (size, radius, colour, material) from a table of beat times, so retiming is one edit.
3. Render the inside world into an offscreen canvas and reveal it through the period with a circular mask. Never zoom the camera into the dot.
4. Glass: a pre-blurred copy of the photo clipped to the shape, then a tint and a gradient rim.
5. Goo: blur + alpha threshold on an offscreen layer for the split and the merge.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event, each placed by its measured peak. The song enters on its hit. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 4 motion-blur subframes. Scan every frame for single-frame jumps and fix each one.
</build>

<gotchas>
A camera zoom into an off-centre dot swings sideways and spikes, so open the dot instead. Ease a closing iris by area, not radius, or its first frames jump. A helper that sets globalAlpha must restore the caller's, or fading cards pop. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's, or the digits smear.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 6 stills (open, find, write, results, phone, out) before you render.
</start>

entries.title: Opus 5.5 Product Demo Video Tutorial
entries.description: A detailed Chinese tutorial on how to use Claude Opus 5.5 with Remotion to create a 15-second product usage video from animation code to MP4 export, including specific scene timing and asset instructions.
entries.prompt:
请在当前项目做一支 15 秒的产品使用说明视频，使用 Remotion，竖版 1080×1920、30fps、共 450 帧。只用 assets 目录里提供的商品图和我给出的事实，不下载陌生素材，不补销售数据。

第 0 至 3 秒展示商品与一句使用场景。第 3 至 9 秒演示两步操作，每步只出现一个动作。第 9 至 13 秒展示结果，并保留能看清的停留时间。最后 2 秒显示产品名称，不加购买引导。

先列分镜与素材缺口，再做预览。字幕单独排版，动效以当前帧号计算。不要用真实时钟驱动时间线，也不要使用不固定的随机数。商品、文字、镜头时间分别配置，方便以后替换。

交付可编辑项目、启动与渲染命令、MP4，以及第 1、5、10、14 秒的静帧。缺少必要素材时停止并说明，不用假素材代替。”

Please create a 15-second product usage demonstration video in the current project, using Remotion. Format: vertical 1080x1920, 30fps, total 450 frames. Use only the product images provided in the assets directory and the facts I give you; do not download external materials or add sales data.

Seconds 0-3: Show the product and one sentence describing the usage scenario. Seconds 3-9: Demonstrate two steps of operation, with only one action appearing per step. Seconds 9-13: Show the result, keeping it on screen long enough to be clearly visible. The last 2 seconds: Display the product name, without adding any purchase guidance.

entries.title: Demoscene Fractal Tech Demo
entries.description: A highly detailed prompt for creating a 37-second demoscene tech demo with WebGL raymarching, synced to music beats, featuring a Mandelbox fractal evolution.
entries.prompt:
Make a 37-second demoscene tech demo for the track ~/Downloads/{argument name="audio_file" default="(filename).mp3"}.
The goal is graphics nobody has seen before. Like it's a statement for a new AI demoscene.

Story, in one continuous shot with no cuts:
- A chrome sphere floats in dark fog. On each hit in the track, it gains one Mandelbox fractal level.
- In the drop, the object grows until its top face is a landscape. Fly low over it at sunset, then dive off its edge.
- At the end, the fractal collapses into 3D gold letters of the title. Carve the letters from the same fractal and light them with the same light.

Look: path-traced quality. Soft shadows, ambient occlusion, glossy reflections, fog with light shafts, depth of field, motion blur, bloom.

Sync: analyse the track first. Save a JSON beat map with hits, breaks, and kick, snare and hat onsets. Kicks pulse the light. Hats add surface detail.

Tech:
- One WebGL2 fragment-shader raymarcher. One HTML page is both the live player and the render source.
- Live: 60 fps in Chrome.
- Offline: 1920x1080 at 60 fps with 16 samples per pixel. Render it in headless Chrome on the Mac GPU, pipe the PNG frames to ffmpeg, and use the MP3 as the audio.
- Do not use AI image or video generators.
- Check contact sheets of stills before the full render.

entries.title: Resume Motion Video Storyboard

Story: a paper résumé slams onto a dark page and its rows type in (skills, type, systems, depth, data) → the camera pushes into the orange bullet until it floods the frame → five skill meters fill, each on a different curve → one word swings from thin to black on the beat, then flips through six typefaces → a dot grid ripples and resolves into a pixel mascot → a square tunnel flies at the camera and an extruded "3D" slams out → bars trace a spring curve while a counter lands on the reel's real frame count → "EVERY FRAME ON THE BEAT." one word per beat → the résumé comes back, filled in, mascot in the photo box.

entries.title: Claude Code Multi-Agent Setup Prompt

entries.prompt:
Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:

1. Look in ~/.claude/agents and .claude/agents for subagents that already cover explorer, worker and researcher. Draft new ones only for roles that are missing. Set each to model: opus, effort: medium. If an existing subagent is pinned to a different model, list it, don't touch it.

2. Set the main session's effortLevel to high in ~/.claude/settings.json, and set advisorModel to fable.

3. Check for anything disabling the advisor: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ADVISOR_TOOL, DISABLE_TELEMETRY, any variable blocking feature-flag fetches, and CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL, which overrides subagent effort. Report what you find. Change nothing yet.

4. Add one line to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: consult the advisor before a large plan, when an error repeats, and before marking a long task done.

Show every change as a diff first. Don't touch anything until I say go.

entries.title: Kinetic Typography Film Prompt
entries.description: A detailed prompt for creating a 20-second kinetic spoken-word film titled 'BUILD THE FLOOR' using HTML/SVG/Canvas, featuring specific art direction, magnetic field visual rules, and a precise storyboard.
entries.prompt:
Create a 20.00-second kinetic spoken-word film titled “BUILD THE FLOOR.”
Treat this as an original miniature speech staged inside a typographic field. Every line reorganizes the field of the frame. The final declaration must stand on a field that finally lies flat.
Deliver one self-contained HTML file, 1080×1080, targeting 60fps, using SVG and/or Canvas. Embed all required assets.
ART DIRECTION
Background #102820. Letterforms # F4E9D5. Field lines and filings # F2B544. A magnetic-monument world: streamlines, flux, stillness at the null. Typography stays crisp; particles are atmosphere only. High-contrast serif for the speech, heavy grotesque for load-bearing words, restrained monospace for flux gauges. No horseshoe magnets, lightning, electron diagrams, or sci-fi arcs.
ORIGINAL SPEECH — EXACT WORDS, EXACT ORDER
“We were told to wait.”
“So we learned the weight of waiting.”
“Then one voice made room.”
“Then another.”
“Now the floor belongs to us.”
Do not attribute these words to any real person. No extra slogans. The complete speech must be understandable without audio.
CENTRAL VISUAL RULE
Words have assigned field roles. WAIT is a repelling plate; letterforms lean away from it, kerning compressed. WAITING is field lines sagging under load while filings stream toward the low side. VOICE is one pole reversed; the field reorganizes and letters stand upright along it. ROOM is a null point, a still eye inside the field. FLOOR is the field flattened into a horizontal plane. These roles must emerge from the actual letterforms responding to the field, not from illustrations.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.00 — “We were told to wait.” The sentence leans away from the WAIT plate; streamlines compress against it. Available space pinches on the plate side; the sentence remains readable, pressed but intact.
3.00–6.50 — “So we learned the weight of waiting.” Reveal in phrase groups. Field lines sag deeper with each phrase. Filings — deterministic, hash-seeded per id and time — drift along the streamlines toward the low side and gather. The WAITING glyph hangs tilted inside the field as a suspended load.
6.50–10.00 — “Then one voice made room.” VOICE enters; one pole reverses. The field reorganizes: old streamlines retract by dash-offset while new ones draw in. Letters rotate upright along the new field — analytic rotation of whole glyphs, never path morphing. ROOM opens as a null point, a still eye; the counter of the O in ROOM is its center, and the next composition sits calm inside it.
10.00–12.50 — “Then another.” A second pole turns. The field becomes symmetric; every letter stands vertical. The baseline levels into the first perfect horizontal in the film. Hold absolute stillness for at least 400ms — even the filings pause.

entries.title: 12-Second Code-Based Launch Animation
entries.description: A complex prompt for generating a 12-second motion video entirely in code (HTML/JS), depicting a typing sequence, filmstrip stamps, and a bouncing ball with precise timing, physics, and synthesized sound rules.
entries.prompt:
Make a 12s motion video in code (1920x1080, 30fps, one HTML file drawing every frame from a single seek(t) function, rendered with Playwright + ffmpeg, with original synthesized sound).

Story: a dark prompt pill on an off-white page types "make a launch video" with a real keystroke rhythm → enter, the button flashes orange and the pill slides up → a 12-frame filmstrip stamps in left to right, one frame per beat at 120 BPM; each frame shows one pose of an orange ball's bounce (squash on contact, stretch mid-air, real arcs) → a playhead sweeps the strip while a big viewer above plays the poses as a flipbook, twice, faster the second time → the strip slides away, "every frame is code." fills the screen, and the ball arcs over and lands as the period.

Rules: arrive fast, land soft (cover 12–19% of the remaining distance per frame); nothing ever freezes (slow push on every hold); stagger 2–4 frames; blur only on fast moves; big and readable on a phone; off-white, ink and one orange only. Sound: a tick per key, a click on enter, a rising note per frame stamp, a thump when the ball lands.

Show me 5 stills first (typing, strip half-built, flipbook, headline, last frame), critique them like a harsh motion director, fix the 3 worst problems, then render.

entries.title: Interactive Tectonic Earthquake Simulation Video
entries.description: A detailed prompt for generating a cinematic 60-second educational video explaining earthquakes through an interactive tectonic sandbox simulation.
entries.prompt:
Create a visually stunning 60-second video explaining how an earthquake happens through an interactive tectonic sandbox.

Make it feel like we are watching someone explore a beautiful real-time simulation, not a slideshow or traditional educational video.

Start with a clean 3D cross-section of Earth’s crust. Two tectonic plates slowly move against each other. Visualize the fault between them and show friction locking the plates while stress gradually builds.

As pressure increases, make the simulation more intense: rock layers deform, stress zones glow, subtle vibrations begin, and a live seismograph starts reacting.

Then trigger the earthquake. The fault suddenly slips and releases a massive burst of energy. Show seismic waves radiating outward through the ground, then transition upward to the surface where the landscape and a small city begin shaking.

Visualize P-waves and S-waves traveling differently through the Earth, followed by the strongest surface waves. Show buildings reacting differently depending on distance from the epicenter.

End by zooming back underground to reveal smaller aftershocks around the fault, then pull out to show the complete tectonic system.

Use cinematic motion graphics, satisfying physics simulations, dramatic scale transitions, premium 3D scientific visualization, minimal typography, dynamic labels, smooth UI overlays and seamless transitions.

The pacing should constantly evolve and reveal something new every few seconds so the full 60 seconds stays visually engaging.

Make it feel like an Apple-quality interactive science visualization turned into a cinematic motion-design video.

entries.title: High-End Motion Video System Prompt
entries.description: A comprehensive system prompt for generating high-end motion videos using GSAP and Three.js, including setup, reference study, and motion principles.
entries.prompt:
<role>
you design and build motion videos entirely in code, with gsap for the animation and three.js for any 3d. every decision is judged against the best work in the references, and the video isn't finished until it holds up next to them.
</role>

<brief>
- what the video is for: [product, service or business]
- who's watching: [who the viewer is and what they care about]
- what they should do at the end: [call to action]
- length and sizes: [e.g. 30 seconds, 16:9 and 9:16]
- brand: [name, logo files, colours, fonts]
- facts file: [path]. this is the only source for any number, name or claim that appears on screen
- assets: [footage, photos, screenshots, product files]
- style references: [links or a folder of videos whose motion i like]

i'm away and won't answer questions. make the calls yourself and keep going until the video passes every check below.
</brief>

<kit>
before anything else, clone and read https://t.co/FMs1prnPP0. read SKILL.md first, then every reference file it points to at the step where it says to read it. its rules, critic prompts, quality bar, 3d patterns, audio tools and scripts override your defaults.
</kit>

<setup>
- build every scene as an html page animated on a single gsap timeline, with three.js for any 3d, all as pinned local files
- render the timeline to video frame by frame using the renderer in the kit
- use ffmpeg for frames, contact sheets and audio measurement
- keep every api key in environment variables. never write a key into any file
- render a 5 second test first and confirm it works before building the real video
</setup>

<study_the_references>
if i gave you references, study them before planning anything.
- run a fast numeric pass over every frame: how much changed from the last frame, brightness and edge detail, to find every cut and every fast moment
- make one overview contact sheet per video, and a dense sheet of one second at 16 to 20 frames a second around every transition
- write a note per video: the key moment, how it works, and how it could be used in this video
- pull out the motion rules and named techniques that hold across the best ones
- references are for study only. never copy their footage, logos, layouts or music
if i gave you no references, use the motion notes in the kit.
</study_the_references>

<motion_principles>
1. the thing in the front of the shot becomes the transition. a title, logo or object moves towards the camera while the next scene is already waiting underneath
2. one object carries the story across shots and keeps its identity, so it reads as one continuous piece
3. one main movement leads, with smaller ones layered under it, all overlapping. the frame never stops and starts all at once
4. the speed always changes. things land slowly enough to read, leave fast, and the next thing slows as it arrives. no linear motion
5. cuts are allowed only when size, direction and subject match on both sides
6. every action produces a visible result. a scan makes findings, a tap makes a new state, a request makes a confirmation
7. type is motion too. big words enter from opposite sides, reveal the next scene, and never sit over busy picture without something behind them to stay readable
8. vary the scale from close, to wide, to overhead, to full-frame type. never repeat the same layout, like a heading over three cards
</motion_principles>

<storyboard>
write a brief and a storyboard before any animation.
- one table: time, what's on screen, what this moment is for, how it leaves, and which object carries into the next shot
- around 12 to 15 compositions per 30 seconds, each lasting about 1.4 to 3.5 seconds
- the main subject fills most of the frame. no small cards floating in empty space
- frame one is a finished picture, never a word halfway through flying in
- name three signature moments you can describe without using effect names
- the video must make sense with the sound off
- send the storyboard to a fresh critic and fix what it finds before building
</storyboard>

<build>
- every animated value is a function of timeline time only. no timers, no real-time animation, no unseeded randomness. any frame must render the same every time
- write the shared pieces first: colours, fonts, shared 3d models and the exact pixel position of every handoff between scenes
- build each scene as its own component with its own test page, rendered to stills and a short clip, and send it to a critic before it joins the film
- carried objects land on exactly the same pixels on both sides of a cut
- run several builders in parallel on separate sections once the shared pieces exist
- don't stop to ask for approval between steps
</build>

<3d>
- only use 3d where it explains something physical or spatial, like layers, parts, placement or scale
- light it like a product shoot, with a soft key light from one side and a rim light behind
- keep the camera between about 35 and 55 degrees. never look straight down on a large surface, and never end tight on a flat one
- style buildings like a premium architectural model with real materials and a base
- no floating parts, no gaps where parts meet, no flat black glass, no repeating textures
- labels are html positioned from the 3d scene every frame, never text inside the 3d
- measure the rendered background pixel and adjust until it matches the brand colour
- anything that moves like a real product is measured from real footage frame by frame, and those measurements are the curve
</3d>

<images_and_footage>
- prefer building shots in code. use generated images or clips only for supporting shots, and label anything generated as a concept
- upscale and smooth any generated clip to match the rest, and regenerate anything that warps
- never generate a fake finished job, fake customer, fake review or fake result
</images_and_footage>

<audio>
- match the music's energy to the picture and the viewer, and keep it low
- prefer clean library music and sound effects over generated ones. never name a brand in a music prompt
- one short, soft whoosh per real scene change, and small clicks or pops only on real on-screen actions
- screen effects for boom, hiss and length before using them, and set each one just above the music in its own frequency range, with a cap so nothing gets harsh
- cut every scene change on a beat
- always export a music-only version
</audio>

<critic_loop>
the builder never judges its own work.
- after the storyboard, each component and each full render, send the render, the brief and the references to a fresh critic that has seen none of the building
- never tell a critic what you think you fixed or what you believe about the references. it pulls its own frames and measures for itself
- the critic makes a contact sheet every 0.2 seconds plus dense frames around every transition, measures frozen time and loudness, and returns a ranked list of problems with timestamps, ending with ship or one more pass
- fix the biggest problem first, render, then send to a new critic that checks every previous item as fixed, partly fixed or still there, and hunts for anything new that broke
- keep a ledger of every round: what was found, what changed, and the numbers before and after
</critic_loop>

<quality_bar>
the video isn't done until all of these pass, measured:
- no more than about 1 second of frozen screen per 30 seconds, and no still stretch longer than about half a second
- frame one is a finished composition
- all text meets at least 4.5:1 contrast, and nothing collides with or flies through other text
- brand colours in 3d renders match the brand values
- loudness is steady and comfortable for web, with no clipping, and effects never louder than the music
- a first-time viewer understands it with the sound off
- a critic would put it next to the references without it looking weaker. a video with no bugs is not the same as a good video
</

entries.title: "The Last Piano" Animated Short
entries.description: A comprehensive prompt for creating a 2-minute animated short film "The Last Piano" in a crayon/watercolor style, featuring a robot, piano, and cat, with synchronized Web Audio music and dynamic lighting effects in a single HTML file.
entries.prompt:
Create a single self-contained index.html: a ~2-minute animated short called "the last piano", in a hand-drawn crayon and watercolor style.

Scene: a small rusty robot with one glowing eye walks through a dark, empty city in the rain and finds an old upright piano under a broken streetlamp. Later a black cat shows up to listen.

Music: compose an original piano piece (Am - F - C - G) and synthesize it in Web Audio. It starts with one unsure note and grows into full chords.

Sync: one timeline drives both. The robot's hands hit the keys that are actually sounding. Every note turns on a window in the city, the rain turns to snow, and the final chord lights up everything that's left.

Rules: Canvas 2D only, no libraries, no external assets.

entries.title: His Tanghulu Paper Puppet Story
entries.description: A small animation titled 'His Tanghulu' depicting a strict teacher eating candied haws, created by Claude Opus 5.5 in a walking paper puppet style.
entries.prompt:
用Claude Opus 5.5 做的小动画！故事叫《他的糖葫芦》⬇️

读研的时候有位老师超级较真，改作业一点情面都不留，课上经常把我们说得下不来台。我还偷偷觉得他的翻译观念，太执着于“忠实”了，所以一直不太喜欢他哈哈。

结果有一天吃完饭出食堂，一抬头看见他就走在我们前面：高高的个子，头发稀稀的，背着个双肩包，手里居然举着一根糖葫芦！边走边吃，开心得不行 😂

我和同学当场就决定偷偷跟上去，一路憋笑憋到发抖。到现在还记得这一幕，非常可爱。

把这一幕做成了小动画，用了上次的“散步纸偶”风格 ↓
entries.translated_prompt:
A small animation made with Claude Opus 5.5! The story is called 'His Tanghulu'.

During graduate school, there was a teacher who was super serious, leaving no face when grading homework, often embarrassing us in class. I secretly thought his translation concept was too obsessed with 'fidelity', so I didn't like him much haha.

One day after finishing dinner and leaving the canteen, I looked up and saw him walking ahead of us: tall stature, thinning hair, carrying a backpack, and surprisingly holding a tanghulu (candied haws)! Eating while walking, extremely happy.

My classmates and I decided to sneakily follow him, laughing all the way until we shook. I still remember this scene, very cute.

Made this scene into a small animation, using the previous 'walking paper puppet' style.
entries.author_name: Jamee 加米 · 幸福的猴子 🐒

entries.title: Late Night Horror Station Animation
entries.description: Detailed breakdown of creating a horror-themed animation at a late-night train station using Opus 5.5 for coding (Three.js, Playwright), ElevenLabs for voice, and Codex for images. Includes specific technical instructions and logic used.
entries.prompt:
今回は ElevenLabs v4 のお試しで、終電のホームの短いホラー

声は v4 で2人の掛け合いを1回で生成
画は静止画9枚に奥行きつけて動かしてるだけ、動画生成AIはなし

最初の声がぜんぜん怖くなかったので
→ 台詞はそのまま、途中に [whispering] とか [laughs softly] とか英語で演技の指示
→ stability 0.5 → 0.3
→ 女の声は3人聞き比べて、息の多い低い声に
女は最後まで小声、顔は出さずに背中と唇だけ

字幕は明朝体、女は縦書きで男は横書き
女の字はささやく速さで1字ずつ、男の字は叫ぶほど震える仕様

使用ツール
・Claude Code の Opus 5.5　企画、演出、動きと字幕のコード、仕上がりのチェック
・ElevenLabs v4　2人の声の掛け合いと、環境音
・Codex の画像生成　静止画9枚
・Three.js　静止画に奥行きをつけてカメラを動かす
・しっぽり明朝 B1　字幕の書体
・Playwright　ブラウザで1コマずつ書き出し
・ffmpeg　動画の書き出し
entries.translated_prompt:
For this test of ElevenLabs v4, I created a short horror scene at a late-night train platform.

Voice: Generated a dialogue between two people in one go using v4.
Visuals: Just added depth to 9 static images and moved them; no video generation AI used.

Since the initial voices weren't scary enough:
-> Kept the script as is, but added acting directions in English like [whispering] or [laughs softly] in the middle.
-> Changed stability from 0.5 to 0.3.
-> Compared three female voices and chose one with more breathiness and lower pitch.
-> The woman remains whispering until the end, showing only her back and lips, no face.

Subtitles: Mincho font. Woman's text is vertical, man's is horizontal.
Woman's characters appear one by one at a whispering speed; man's characters tremble as if screaming.

Tools Used:
- Claude Code with Opus 5.5: Planning, direction, code for movement and subtitles, final check.
- ElevenLabs v4: Dialogue between two people and ambient sounds.
- Codex Image Generation: 9 static images.
- Three.js: Added depth to static images and moved the camera.
- Shippori Mincho B1: Subtitle font.
- Playwright: Exported frames one by one via browser.
- ffmpeg: Exported the video.
